speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUESTS FOR POLICE REINFORCEMENTS AND JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house would wish to know that late last week I received two telegrams from the premier of Newfoundland, the first regarding a request that 50 additional Royal Canadian Mounted Police constables be sent to that province, and the second requesting the setting up of a judicial inquiry into the troubles that have occurred there.
While this government has no intention of infringing on matters under provincial jurisdiction, I feel impelled to say that the premier of Newfoundland has greatly aggravated the present situation in that province by intervening in a labour dispute in a way which apparently goes beyond the usual role of government. The result, as might have been anticipated, has been a violent reaction on the part of the workers concerned. Under the circumstances we have concluded that it would be provocative and likely to cause further outbreaks of violence to authorize the sending of further members of the R.C.-M.P. at this time.
We feel that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has performed its duty with fairness and efficiency. The situation in Newfoundland will be kept constantly under review and if the mounted police, in the proper discharge of their duties, are subject to or encounter intimidation or threats by lawbreakers reconsideration will be given immediately to this decision.
With regard to the request that a commissioner be appointed to inquire into and assess responsibility for acts of lawlessness and violence in Newfoundland, there seems 66968-9-1244
to be no necessity for the setting up of such a commission. I feel I speak for all hon. members in this house when I say that the important consideration now is not to have a commission or any other inquiry set up to determine a responsibility which is so apparent. The important thing and the urgent necessity at the present time is to bring about an end to the existing situation. I would think that the danger of disorder and violence would be very much reduced if all those concerned would agree to a cooling off period of say two weeks. The whole country, I am sure, would welcome some reasonable action being taken along these lines.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUESTS FOR POLICE REINFORCEMENTS AND JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret to have to advise the house that I have received a letter dated March 12 from the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in which he submits his resignation. I have advised the commissioner by letter today that under the circumstances I have no alternative but to accept his decision and will prepare a submission accordingly to the governor in council. 1 will ask consent of the house to have these letters printed as an appendix to today's Hansard.
The facts leading up to this resignation can be summarized as follows. On Sunday, March 8, I received a wire from the attorney general of Newfoundland asking for 50 additional Royal Canadian Mounted Police reinforcements and citing the terms of the contract. I immediately consulted with Commissioner Nicholson and found that he in turn had been advised by Superintendent Parsons, the officer commanding the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in Newfoundland, that he had made a request to the attorney general of Newfoundland.
As a result of these consultations, however, it was agreed that the situation might be kept under control by the sending of some 25 members of the Newfoundland constabulary from the city of St. John's into the strike area. This was done, and a further 20 Royal Canadian Mounted Police from
1960	HOUSE OF
Newfoundland-Administration of Justice other points in the divisional area were also brought into the strike area and, on this basis, it was reported that control of the situation might be maintained. However, arrangements were made by the commissioner, with my approval, to alert the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in the other maritime provinces so that if the situation should require it and authority should be forthcoming, reinforcements could be sent in from the outside with a minimum of delay. This information was accordingly conveyed by the commissioner to Superintendent Parsons and by him to the attorney general of Newfoundland.
Following the clash that took place on the highway outside the town of Badger on Tuesday evening, March 10, the situation apparently deteriorated further and Superintendent Parsons advised the commissioner that in view of the movement of 100 further strikers into the area, he felt that the call for reinforcements should be renewed.
On receipt of this information from the commissioner on Wednesday morning, I approved his taking the steps necessary to gather the men in the maritimes who had been alerted, and to have air transportation arranged. I told him, however, that while these steps were to be taken as a precaution I was not giving authority for the plane to take off from Moncton, and that this was not to take place until I had an opportunity to consider the situation further and to consult with my colleagues with regard to it. These consultations were held on Wednesday afternoon, and it was decided that a state of readiness should be maintained but that reinforcements should not be dispatched at that time.
The commissioner thereupon informed me that he could not agree with the decision, in view of his understanding of the effect of the contract, and that he would have to resign. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I might stop here to say that the decision of the commissioner has been under review. I do not want to give the appearance that this was immediately precipitated; it has been under review, and the final decision has been taken and communicated by my letter to him today to which I have already referred.
In order that the issue may be clearly understood, I should read the relevant clause, which is clause 13 of the contract, as follows:
13. Where in the opinion of the attorney general of the province an emergency exists within the province requiring additional members of the force to assist in dealing with such emergency, Canada shall, at the request of the attorney general of the province addressed to the commissioner, increase the strength of the division as requested if, in the opinion of the Attorney General of


Canada, having regard to other responsibilities and duties of the force, such increase is possible.
This, in my view, makes it clear that before the government of Canada is required to dispatch reinforcements as requested, the Attorney General of Canada must form the opinion that, having regard to other responsibilities and duties of the force, it is possible to send the reinforcements. It is also clear that the ultimate responsibility for the decision rests on the Attorney General of Canada.
Further to clarify the issue leading up to this resignation, I think I should read at this point the relevant passages from the commissioner's letter. I am now quoting from his letter of March 12:
There is no doubt in my mind as to the need and I am certain that the number of men asked for can be provided without prejudice to "other responsibilities and duties".
I realize that other issues are before you which arise from this strike but I feel most strongly that the matter of law enforcement should be isolated and dealt with on its own merits. This is the attitude the force has taken throughout. It has not concerned itself with the issues back of the strike but has merely tried to maintain law and order in the area.
I think the contract clause on this matter of providing reinforcements in an emergency is clear and I cannot escape the conclusion that failure to supply reinforcements in this instance is a breach of that clause. Bearing in mind that we have similar contracts with seven other provinces the decision of the government has a particular significance.
With these considerations in mind I feel I have no option but to ask you to accept my resignation and this I now do. I hope you will be able to relieve me as soon as possible and I shall await your advice as to what arrangements will be made to that end.
I cannot close without telling you how much I regret having to take this step. I am within a year of completing my full service and I had looked forward to finishing my time in a more pleasant way. I have enjoyed serving under your direction and I have appreciated your support of the force and your active interest and understanding in all aspects of its work. I assure you that it is only a firm conviction of the correctness of my view which leads me to take this disagreeable action.
That is the end of the quotation from the commissioner's letter. I have reproduced in quotes those parts in which the commissioner discussed the issue between us. As I said, I shall ask leave to table the whole letter and my reply.
It was with deep regeret that I found that the commissioner disagrees with the decision that I felt had to be taken, and that this disagreement led him to decide that he should resign. The fact is, however, that the contract is a contract between the government of Newfoundland and the government of Canada, and that the decision called for by

the contract is a decision to be made by the Attorney General of Canada.
In acknowledging the commissioner's letter of resignation I have endeavoured to set out the position, as I understand it, in the light of clause 13, as follows:
The obligation imposed on Canada by that clause is to increase the number of members of the force in the province if, in my opinion as Attorney General of Canada, "having regard to other responsibilities	and	duties of	the	force", such
increase is possible.
In reaching	my	conclusion	on	the questionwhether "having regard to other responsibilities and duties of the force" such increase were possible, I, of course, as you know, gave the most careful and anxious consideration to your views that additional members could and should be sent to Newfoundland without prejudice to other responsibilities	and	duties of	the	force. However, upon a consideration of all the factors, including especially	the importance of preserving the character and capacity of the force to discharge its duty in connection with law enforcement in all of Canada, I came to the conclusion, after consulting my colleagues, that, as the situation existed at that time, it was not possible to send the additional men requested without prejudicing the other responsibilities and duties of the force. This decision was my responsibility. I reached it only after the most careful consideration of your views and of all the other factors that, in my judgment, were relevant. I regret profoundly that you came to the conclusion that, by reason of that decision, you should resign.
That is the end of the quotation from my letter.
Since it is obvious that the point involved here is the question of whether account should be taken of anything more than the mere physical availability of men in determining whether reinforcements should be sent, I should outline the view upon which my decision is based.
I do not accept, and the government of Canada cannot accept, that an issue of this importance-whether reinforcements should be sent under the circumstances such as existed here-can be decided on the basis of a mere mathematical calculation as to whether men are physically available. We cannot discharge our responsibility by considering only the physical circumstances prevailing and examining the need for men under those circumstances. We must also consider the over-all responsibilities of the force, and our responsibility for the force, in a much wider context.
The primary duty of the force is to maintain law and order wherever the force operates throughout Canada. It is therefore an essential responsibility of the force to maintain its full integrity and its ability to discharge that duty on a national basis. In my view I cannot overlook, in assessing the responsibilities of the force, the necessity to ensure that it is not cast in a role which in effect
Newfoundland-[DOT]Administration of Justice might disable it from discharging its responsibilities to the country as a whole by weakening its standing as a law enforcement body. The responsibility of the force in this sense I have had to keep very much in mind in assessing the request which came from Newfoundland.
The Prime Minister has in his statement indicated clearly our views as to where overall responsibility for creating this situation lies, and also what should be done now to end it. It will be apparent from the Prime Minister's statement what are the various factors that I have had to bear in mind in assessing this call for reinforcements.
In the current situation the activities of the government of Newfoundland appear to have gone beyond the usual role of a government. That role in this context is first to provide the machinery for the promotion of industrial peace and development and for the settlement of industrial disputes, and second to preserve and enforce law and order in the course of any dispute that may arise.
In the current situation, however, the activities of the Newfoundland government take on the character of an intervention in a dispute actually in progress, on the side of one of the parties and against the union which up to that time had been chosen as the bargaining agent by the workers and certified as such under the terms of the appropriate provincial legislation. This is an abnormal role for a government, and certainly has the elements of an attempt to extinguish from the province a trade union national in character and hitherto chosen by the workers in that industry, in that province, as their bargaining agent.
As I appreciate the situation, therefore, the request made by the government of Newfoundland for Royal Canadian Mounted Police reinforcements takes on the character not of a request to assist in the normal function and duty of the province in maintaining law and order, but of a request for additional help made necessary in the course of the furtherance of a project to extinguish a union from the province.
We have also had to bear in mind the possibility that under these circumstances to send additional Royal Canadian Mounted Police into Newfoundland, instead of ensuring that the situation is kept under control, might act only as provocation to further incidents of violence and defiance, so there is no certainty that the sending of them would not do more to inflame the situation than to control it.
After weighing all these factors, and discussing them with my colleagues, I have come to the conclusion that the arguments against

Newfoundland-Administration of Justice sending more men at this time outweigh the arguments in favour, and I have decided accordingly, having regard to all the responsibilities and duties of the force.
This decision, as I have said, was a decision which was my responsibility to make, and I regret that the decision was not acceptable to the commissioner; but I had no alternative but to make it, and having made it to accept his resignation if he felt he should submit it. The situation, however, will be continuously watched and arrangements are being maintained with regard to the alert of the men in the other maritime provinces. As the Prime Minister has said, reinforcements will be sent immediately should they become necessary in order to protect the safety of the members of the force who are presently engaged in their proper function of maintaining law and order in Newfoundland.
It remains only for me to express my deep, personal regret that the commissioner should have felt impelled to act as he has done. Hon. gentlemen will perhaps appreciate my attitude in this regard, particularly in the light of the close personal relationship which has existed, and of my knowledge that the commissioner is within a year of normal retirement. As I have said in my letter to him, although I disagree fundamentally with his view as to the course which he should follow, I respect his sincerity in arriving at his decision.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUESTS FOR POLICE REINFORCEMENTS AND JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin by saying that I think all members on all sides of the house will have learned with the greatest possible regret of the resignation of the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. He has served his country for many years with honour and distinction, and he has always shown in that service- and I know the minister will agree with me -a high sense of public responsibility and duty. I feel quite certain that the commissioner would not have resigned for any reason which is inconsistent with his own sense of public duty and responsibility, and in the communications from which the minister has read the commissioner has indicated in quite clear terms his reason for this resignation.
There are one or two other matters, Mr. Speaker, on which I would like to comment. The first is the decision announced by the Prime Minister and elaborated on by the minister, not to accede to the request for police reinforcements made by the government of Newfoundland in accordance with section 13 of the agreement entered into on June 12, 1957 between the governments of Canada and Newfoundland. That section is perfectly clear. I do not need to read it

again; it has been put on the record once more this afternoon by the minister. The only question to be determined by the Attorney General of Canada under that section is whether the requested increase is possible having regard to other responsibilities and duties of the force.
The minister this afternoon, in making his statement, has given an interpretation of section 13 which will certainly require, and will receive, very careful examination. It was an interpretation which, although I tried to follow it, was difficult for me to understand. He related his decision to the activities of the government of Newfoundland, not so much to the request of that government for further assistance in the maintenance of law and order but because of an interpretation- and this is his responsibility, not that of the government-which he has given to certain policies of the government of Newfoundland. The minister has taken his responsibility in that regard and has decided that in view of this kind of interpretation given to a paragraph that on the face of it seems very clear he is not able to accede to a request made within the terms of an agreement reached with the province.
I also wish to discuss the matter of the request of the government of the province of Newfoundland for a public inquiry. I hope the Prime Minister will table or put in Hansard the exchange between the premier of Newfoundland and himself, the request and the reply to the request. I have not a copy of the request made by the premier, nor have I seen it except in the press. However, it would appear from the press that the request for a public inquiry was made in the following terms:
In the interest of the peace, order and good government of Canada, and to protect the good name of the R.C.M.P., the government of Newfoundland invites the government of Canada to set up at once a public inquiry.
Mr. Smallwood is reported by the press as having asked that the inquiry be made under a superior court judge from outside Newfoundland to investigate the "acts of lawlessness and violence which have taken place in central Newfoundland since the strike of the loggers began on December 31". The inquiry, according to the press, should be held "for the purpose of ascertaining the facts and assessing the responsibility".
In the first place I think the fact that such a request was made in those terms is an evidence of the desire of the government of Newfoundland to secure and make public all the facts concerned with the matter covered by this inquiry. We on this side of the house have thought that a full and objective inquiry of this kind would be

desirable in view of the uncertainty created and the differences of opinion that have been expressed over what actually happened. The conduct of the R.C.M.P. has been bitterly attacked in the press and elsewhere and as strongly defended. Charges of disorder and violence have been made and have been rejected. I suggest that if we desire to understand the situation, as we do, and if we wish to criticize recent legislation passed in the house of assembly of Newfoundland in meeting the situation, we should have accurate and full information from an objective and impartial inquiry on which to base our views.
Any differences of opinion over facts are bound to have a bearing on differences of opinion over the legislation which was passed by all the members of both parties in the Newfoundland legislative assembly, which was and which remains accountable to the people of Newfoundland. It will be remembered that last summer the federal government initiated legislation in this house, which was approved by parliament and by all hon. members of this party, and which ended a strike and sent men back to work. This was, of course, an interference with the right of free, collective bargaining.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUESTS FOR POLICE REINFORCEMENTS AND JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman say that the legislation in Newfoundland is comparable?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUESTS FOR POLICE REINFORCEMENTS AND JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
I have not said that, Mr. Speaker, but I have said that we passed legislation in this parliament last summer which was an interference with the right of free, collective bargaining, in that by legislative enactment it sent men back to work. Any interference of that kind can only be justified after all the facts are known, as I think they were known last summer, on grounds of emergency; when the public interest or the public security demands such emergency action in the face of clear and present danger to security or to the economic life of the country or of a province.
On the basis of the facts that are known with regard to the Newfoundland situation strong differences of opinion, as was inevitable, have developed over the measures taken by the government and the legislature of Newfoundland to deal with the situation which confronted that province. I have expressed my own views on this issue when I said in view of recent events in Newfoundland; I wished to repeat what I have already stated, to the effect that the policy of the national Liberal party in labour matters has been and will continue to be firmly based on the right of free, collective bargaining through unions chosen by the workers themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I have said that is the policy of the national Liberal party of Canada, and those words speak for themselves. However, if hon. gentlemen would like to hear it I am prepared to express an opinion. This is the first occasion I have had to speak on this matter in parliament. On the basis of the information I have received I would be unable as leader of this party to agree with certain of the procedures that have been followed or with specific provisions of the new laws.
The people of Newfoundland feel strongly on this matter, and I know that a unanimous assembly with very strong support from the people of that province would not have supported this action of their government if they had not thought-and many of them I am sure came to this conclusion very reluctantly -that the interest and welfare of the province required it. Surely it is our duty not only to get all the facts about this matter but to try and understand the views of the people of Newfoundland with regard to it. I have tried to do that myself, even though as I just said the information I have leads me to conclude that I could not agree with all of the steps taken.
One of the most disquieting features of this whole tragic and unhappy business is the growing sense of grievance and resentment in what is an ancient colony, but a new province, over what so many of its people feel to be a lack of understanding on the mainland of the position; of its difficulties and problems and, indeed, its dangers. This feeling is bound to be increased by the fact that often the conditions, attitudes and circumstances of Newfoundland are not the same as those of the older provinces.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying before the Prime Minister saw fit to interrupt me, the people of Newfoundland are in this matter, as in other matters, naturally sensitive to any misrepresentation of their motives and to anything they consider to be unfair in the reporting of conditions in the province.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, whatever we may think of the action taken in Newfoundland in this labour dispute, it is of vital importance to do nothing to add to this feeling of resentment or to this feeling of being misunderstood; for from that could grow a feeling of isolation which would be especially regrettable as we approach the tenth anniversary of that fortunate day for Canada when the work of confederation was completed by Newfoundland joining this nation. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we all have a responsibility in this parliament, as they have in the legislative assembly of Newfoundland, to refrain from saying or doing anything which would add an unnecessary strain on this union.
I can only add in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that for the reasons I have given it is most regrettable that the kind of objective inquiry requested by the government of Newfoundland, which also would have covered the request made by the Canadian Labour Congress for an inquiry, and which might have had important and positive results along the lines advocated by the Prime Minister himself when he said we ought to have a two-week cooling off period, has been refused by this government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have all been waiting with a great deal of interest to hear a statement on the position of the government with respect to the critical and unfortunate situation in Newfoundland. After hearing the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, I think we can safely say we now know the position of the Conservatives, but I am doubtful whether we know the position of the Liberals; not yet, anyway.
I do want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am not going into the question of the legal interpretation of section 13 of the contract between


the government of Canada and the government of Newfoundland as regards the utilization of the R.C.M. Police in that province; but we do unhesitatingly say that irrespective of the legal interpretation of that matter, in our opinion the position taken by the Minister of Justice is morally a correct one, and we commend him on his decision. He has shown an understanding of the probabilities if certain action had been taken in sending down at this time and under existing circumstances and situation, an additional complement of 50 R.C.M. Police reinforcements. We quite agree with the interpretation which he had the honesty to express just a few moments ago that the request for the reinforcements was not so much on the basis of maintenance of law and order as it was for assistance and as a bulwark in pushing forward the stooge union of the premier of the province of Newfoundland, and we maintain that that is not the purpose and is not the function of the R.C.M. Police.
We are quite disappointed in the statement of the Prime Minister as to the position of his government and as to their decision after reviewing the request for an inquiry. We too feel most strongly that nothing but good could have come from the holding of a judicial inquiry. As was pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition, it is necessary to try to get the absolute and correct facts as to the situation in that province. It would mean a great deal in clearing the air and in clarifying the situation. I repeat that we would ask the Prime Minister to reconsider that decision and have an honest and complete inquiry into the basis of the present situation so far as the dispute in Newfoundland is concerned.
But, sir, though we say that we feel it would be a correct and a useful procedure, we would like to have a little more information also and to know just what is meant or just what is in the Prime Minister's mind when he so emphatically recommends a two-week cooling off period. Just what is meant by a cooling off period, sir? Just what are both sides to the dispute supposed to do? What would take place-

speechtext:
Once again, Mr. Speaker, this motion gives the official opposition an opportunity to comment on a matter of important policy and to criticize, if criticism is required, the action or inaction of the government in respect of that policy. Today, Mr. Speaker, I am going to raise, and I do it in no narrow partisan sense, a question of the greatest importance which concerns our external relations, and a question which has been very much in our minds, indeed which we have been discussing already in some of its aspects. I am referring to the matter of Canadian-United States relations.
I hope in dealing with this matter to do so in as constructive a fashion as possible, and to put some ideas to the government which may help in the solution of some of the problems that face us in this field, and for that purpose to move a motion toward the end of my remarks. I venture to hope, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps this discussion can be carried on without too much reference on one side to the question of what did you do, or perhaps without too much reference on the other side to the question of what did you say. I hope also, Mr. Speaker, that the discussion can proceed without too much display of press clippings and dredging up of debating points from previous occasions, 66968-9-125J
16, 1959	1967
Canadian-United States Relations because the question of Canadian-United States relations is a matter not only of the greatest possible national and international importance, but one which transcends the normal debating points that one makes in specific domestic problems and indeed at times specific problems in international affairs. Therefore I hope to consider this matter with the responsibility which it deserves.
As I said just a moment ago, and have said on many previous occasions, there is no more important subject facing us at the present time than our relations with the United States. I know of no more complicated subject, no subject more difficult or complicated for Canada, politically, economically and indeed culturally; no subject that requires more careful, cool and honest consideration, consideration which will be as free as possible, subject to our human and political weaknesses, from emotion and prejudice and which will be treated with as clear an understanding of where our true long range interest lies, the greatest of which is of course the preservation of peace and security in the world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the problem of our relations with the United States is our most important single international problem, at least in the bilateral sense of the relationship of Canada with any other single country, even though it is only a part, a very important one, of our general international policy for peace and security. I believe that is a point upon which we are all united in this house. This problem is, of course, of far greater importance to Canada than to the United States. I am talking now of the bilateral aspect of our relationship. I do not need to waste the time of the house in elaborating upon it.
The realistic consideration of the problem is often hindered on the one hand by what I might call the unguarded boundary, 140 years of peace approach, which perhaps is less prevalent in Canada than it is in the United States. There it is based upon what many, including myself, have referred to as benevolent ignorance. On the other hand, it does not help in the solution of the problem that faces us in this field when we in Canada display self-righteousness or become oversensitive at times and yield to the temptation to give gratuitous advice to our neighbours occasionally in a fashion which has subjected us to the mild reproach of having become charter members of the international society of sidewalk superintendents.
Both these approaches, on the one side and on the other, prevent the kind of serious consideration of these problems which is required. I suggest, and I am sure my hon. friends will
1968	HOUSE OF
Canadian-United, States Relations agree with me that it is a sign on our part-[DOT] I am talking only about ourselves-of immaturity when we are petulant and captious, when we are purely negative, carping in our criticism, we are not likely to accomplish very much, and we are at a time when there is so much to accomplish in this field.
The keynotes to our relationship with the United States-it may seem platitudinous to say this-are threefold. The first is the intimacy of the relationship, and that speaks for itself. I need say nothing further about that. The evidence of it is at hand on every side in every contact we have with our neighbours across the line. The second keynote is the importance of this relationship and the growing, if you will, awareness of that importance below the line. The third keynote, which in a sense is related to the second and is an aspect of the problem which has been mentioned more than once by the Prime Minister in debates on international affairs, is our interdependence with the United States. This is something of which I believe we are far more conscious than our neighbour is, which may be a fact which helps explain something of the difficulties we have in our relations with the United States.
I should like to remind the house that this matter of interdependence, on which I shall say a few words, should be more than continental, even though it is the continental aspect of interdependence that we so often have in mind when we use the word and even though it is the continental aspect of interdependence of which we are most conscious economically, strategically and politically.
May I just say a word first about the political aspect of this continental interdependence. As reported at page 1549 of Hansard of March 3, the Prime Minister had this to say:
-we intend to continue to assert unswervingly that we shall have for Canada a fair, full and equal participation in all decisions which go to our common defence.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we would be unrealistic if we in this country based our policies on the assumption that we must have equal participation in all decisions that are concerned with common defence.
Would "equitable" have been a better word?

Fair consideration and full consideration, yes; but if we think-and I am sure the Prime Minister will agree with me in this statement-that in all these matters we are going to have equal consideration with the nation which bears the greatest responsibility because it has the greatest power


in the free world, we are going to leave ourselves open to disillusionment which may result in disappointment and, at times, in criticism and complaint. Sovereignty-and the Prime Minister had a good deal to say about this the other day-means equality between states in theory, but it does not and cannot mean absolute equality in practice between states of different size, power and responsibility in reaching decisions of common interest today.
There are recent statements from Washington which prove what I am trying to indicate. There are recent statements which show in an alarming way, I believe-in any event, alarming to me-that the United States government has already made up its mind what to do in certain contingencies that are related to the Berlin situation but which certainly affect the common defence. That defence, we are told-and I am not objecting to the statement because I think it is true-is now and must remain continental in the sense that it cannot be based on national plans or national policies alone. We are told that it must be based on the unity of the two countries for defence planning, or at least for the strategic and tactical side of planning. Yet as President Eisenhower pointed out at his press conference of March 4, and I quote from that conference-and these are words which are pregnant with significance-* When you have got certain circumstances that... could put your nation's life at stake . . . whatever would be necessary the President would then order.
And the measures that he felt it necessary then to order-and I hope he will never be put in the position where he has to do this -nevertheless would affect us just about as much as they would affect the United States of America.
The Prime Minister had something to say about this matter to the House of Commons on March 3 when he said this, and I quote from page 1547 of Hansard:
What is our position in Canada? Some seem to have the view that we could be neutral in any war that may take place, neutral in the event that the United States was involved . . . There is no neutrality of that kind today.
Mr. Speaker, I would not go as far as that, as to insist that we could not be neutral in any war in which the United States was involved, and perhaps the Prime Minister did not mean that.
Under NATO.

Under NATO there is no
neutrality. An attack on one NATO country is an attack on them all. That concept of neutrality we abandoned when we signed the NATO pact in respect of the NATO area,

but I do not think that means that we cannot at least avoid involvement in non-NATO wars that any other country might find itself engaged in in a limited way, or in an area of the world which has nothing to do with NATO.
I am very much interested in this matter. Suppose there was an attack on United States forces in Asia. Then what would our position be?

If there was an attack on
United States forces in the NATO area, of course we would be at war as soon as parliament met and took the necessary action. We have an international obligation to consider an attack on the forces of a NATO country inside the NATO area as an attack on our own forces. If there was an attack on United States forces in some part of the world far removed from the NATO area, in the Far East or some other place, I am not trying to suggest for a minute that we would be able to escape the consequences of any action in which the United States was involved. But I do not go so far, and I have never gone so far and perhaps the Prime Minister would not go so far, as to suggest that this means that we would have to abandon the legal concept of neutrality in any attack on a United States force in any part of the world. I certainly would not want to accept that as a doctrine guiding our international obligations or our international policy.
Yet if the President of the United States ever had to take the kind of action which he mentioned in his press conference, I repeat that we would be affected; we would certainly be involved in some form or other, because we could not escape. The President made clear a week later, on March 4, what he would order in defence against aggression, when he said at the following week's press conference:
We are certainly not going to fight a ground war in Europe.
When I read that statement I wondered. I know it was a statement at a press conference, but it was a statement by the President of the United States, a statement which seems to have been contradicted since then by one or two service chiefs in the United States. But any statement of that kind could not help but create anxiety, I am sure, in the minds of people in other countries who heard it. In the policy leading up to that kind of statement, does Canada have a full, free and equal voice? That is a statement that certainly bears on common defence. What are the implications for Canada of a
Canadian-United States Relations statement of that kind in terms of continental interdependence which we all agree must be recognized?
No doubt we shall have an opportunity to examine these matters in greater detail in subsequent debates on defence. I mention them now merely to point out what I think is one of the major problems facing us in our relations with the United States, namely the increasingly.-perhaps because of the circumstances with which we are faced-one-sided character of continental interdependence in this field and in other fields which I shall mention later.
We agree that policy in defence, trade, production or anything else cannot in this country be based any longer on the old concept of unlimited and unrestricted national sovereignty. I agree wholeheartedly with what the Prime Minister said about that matter the other day. I think there is no doubt where we in this party stand on that matter. We have shown it when we were in office in word and I think we have shown it in deed by our advocacy of NATO and other collective security arrangements. The record of 12 years in office is an indication of where we stand with regard to the matter.
What did the hon. gentleman understand by the swift thinking attributed to the President in that press conference? He mentioned the implications, and then he did not complete the statement.

The implication of that statement which I thought would create some anxiety in people's minds outside the United States-I do not want to say anything which will be unnecessarily alarmist-surely would be that if action were begun in regard to the defence of the rights of the NATO powers in West Berlin, which rights, as the Prime Minister and I have already stated should be firmly upheld, and that action resulted in counteraction, which in turn resulted in conflict, that conflict could only be all-out air conflict.
That is the implication to be drawn from the President's statement. It is of far-reaching importance and underlines the necessity of the fullest, freest and most equal consultation possible among allies before policies of that kind are agreed upon. If the nations of NATO and the free world cling to old, outworn concepts of sovereignty, and by doing so find they have weakened their security and created disunity within the coalition, which apart from the weakening of our strength, is the thing these people would most like to see brought about, we may find that we have saved our sovereignty but lost
1970	HOUSE OF
Canadian-United. States Relations everything else. The Prime Minister put the same idea to us the other day in another way.
I am listening very carefully to the hon. gentleman, and I am asking him for information. What does the hon. gentleman mean by "clinging to the outgrown concept of sovereignty"?

I think the best explanation I can give of my views in that regard is the fact that we considered it necessary in this country ten years ago to accept obligations in regard to collective security which limited our freedom of action. We felt it necessary to give up some of our sovereignty in that respect and accept limits on our freedom of action in order to increase our security and thereby, we hoped, strengthen the peace.
Thank you.

On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, if interdependence-which must, I submit, mean some limitation on sovereignty 

rejects, as I think it should, absolute national sovereignty, then in the continental sense it cannot rest on Canada's excessive subordination to the policies and decisions of the United States. I am now talking about continental interdependence. That is why I strongly believe that Atlantic interdependence is a far better policy and concept for us politically and economically than continental interdependence. Surely we have recognized that in our acceptance of NATO obligations, in the NATO commands, and in everything else which flows from NATO. Surely this means, because of our political situation on this continent, that intercontinental defence for us should include continental defence in the most direct manner possible. Interdependence politically and strategically, as well as economically, I submit is a preferable concept for Canada than continental interdependence.
I know that our relations with the United States in this field recognize this concept of interdependence, but that recognition on such a continental, narrow basis-if the North American continent is a narrow basis; it is only relatively a narrow basis-has surely been shown by the events of the last few years. In some aspects of our relationship that interdependence has been shown to be more apparent than real. We have learned, I think more particularly in the last year or two, that a defence system based on a genuine and equal interdependence of two nations so different in power as are Canada and the United States is very difficult indeed to work out in practice. In practice, whatever we may have in mind in theory, such a system


usually means that the more powerful nation retains most of its independence and the other, the less powerful nation, tends to become more dependent.
May I ask if that has applied in the NATO organization as such, in the hon. member's experience?

I do not think so, Mr. Speaker, because I think the broader the basis of the interdependence the greater opportunity there is for the various members to make their views effectively known. But whether it applies in NATO or not, and I do not think it does to the same extent as bilaterally in the North American continent, surely it is a good thing for Canada to broaden the basis of its interdependence and thereby-I was going to use the word "weaken" the pressures which come from the south when we are working together with the United States alone without the benefit of a larger grouping. This continental relationship, then, which we have to accept and work out to the best of our ability tends to become one more of dependence than interdependence, from our point of view. We have certainly learned in the last few months that this interdependence, this continental interdependence and unity, is more apparent in the field of strategy and planning than it is in the field of development of resources and industrial production.
So is the NATO organization under section 2.

The Prime Minister says this is also so in the NATO organization. But it has not been tested in the same way in that organization because there has not been the same effort yet, that I know of, between any of the NATO countries to work out any special relationship inside NATO, as there has been between Canada and the United States.
Perhaps I know as much as most people how difficult it is to do much about article 2. I think the Canadian delegations at the present time, as in the time of the previous government, have done what they can to make progress in that field. I suggest that the only alternative, Mr. Speaker, is an interdependence which means a balanced, collective defence where each nation can specialize in certain types of defence production. In the long run it seems to me that is the only approach which will make a collective system work, whether that collective system consists of 12, 13 or 14 nations under NATO, or the two nations on the North American continent. If that kind of interdependence is essential this implication must be acceptable by all members of the group,

including the United States, if the collective organization is to survive. It requires defence resource development and production sharing arrangements between governments much more far-reaching than those which now exist between the United States and Canada, and between Canada and the NATO countries.
So much, then, for that aspect of interdependence. What about our trade relations between the two countries? Surely over recent years they have also illustrated our growing dependence on the United States. Hon. members opposite have had a lot to say about that in past years, and they have called attention in no uncertain terms to the dangers to Canada's development because of that growth. I think the growth over the years of our commercial and trade dependence on the United States-I am talking now about the last 10 or 15 years-was not only inevitable, but I think if we had not had that development of economic and trade interdependence we would have been in a very bad way in this country after world war II.
Why did this occur? Why have we become more dependent in these matters on our neighbour? The reasons are pretty obvious, and I am sure are familiar to all members of the house. Perhaps the most important reason, and one we do not often refer to in discussions of this matter, is the fact that we have had two world wars with a relative decline of the western European countries brought about by their efforts and sacrifices during those two world wars. That effort weakened them economically and made them less available as markets for our goods.
The first reason then is the relative decline of the western European countries in the world economics and especially after world war II when there were currency difficulties arising out of impoverishment through war exertions and sacrifices.
Second, there were higher costs of production in North America which tended to divert more and more of our products to the only market where we could compete in price, which was the United States. Third was the important part played by United States capital in our amazing development. We could not have had the pace and pattern of that development without United States capital but it did result in the growing dependence on the United States in some phases of our economy and it resulted also in demands for measures to counter the dangers arising from this kind of development. It has now reached the point in this country where three quarters of the $7,500 billion of the foreign capital invested in Canada comes
Canadian-United States Relations from the United States. This involves an economic and financial problem but it may become a political problem. We need the capital but we want to ensure that the capital does not mean outside control.
A very good illustration of the advantages and dangers of this kind of development which emphasizes our dependence on the United States was given the other day when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke as reported at page 1549 of Hansard of March 3 and had this to say:
How often have hon. gentlemen opposite laughed when we talked of plans for northern development to secure the northern areas for Canada so that they would not be lost.
I do not recall laughing at that policy but we will let that pass. The hon. gentleman continued:
In the last few weeks something of that development plan which was scoffed at, the design of which was to improve the economic future of Canada and also preserve those areas for our defence, has been shown to be achieving fruition in the events which have taken place in connection with those vast mineral and oil areas which are today being taken up.
I believe it is true-the minister directly concerned will correct me if I am wrong; but his own information shows I am not wrong- that this development in the way it has been brought about and is now taking place is largely through the movement of more United States capital through United States oil companies or their Canadian subsidiaries into the northern parts of Canada. This is a recent illustration, a development that has occurred in the last few weeks which reveals the advantages and may later reveal some of the difficulties that flow from that kind of assistance.
Another reason why we have become more dependent on the United States over the years than some of us would perhaps like to see with respect to economic and trade matters is the United States need for our raw and semi-processed material. Hon. members know how this works out. We are advised by the United States when there is a period of emergency in that country where our raw materials are required for strategic or defence purposes, as was the case a few years ago, to develop and produce these resources at any cost and that the market will be there in the United States at an reasonably profitable figure. We are told to go ahead and produce the stuff and then when national production in this country is stepped up or the need diminishes in the United States or as is more often the case, both, the tap is turned off in the United States and restrictions are put on the imports of those goods into Canada, goods that we were urged to produce in the first place.

Canadian-United States Relations
I need only to cite as examples lead, zinc and uranium. It was not many years ago that this country was urged by the United States authorities to proceed with the search for uranium. Washington advised us to search and hunt for all the uranium we could find here and develop it and they would make a contract to purchase practically all of that uranium. We were told it was necessary not only for our economy but for United States security that this should be done. During the period we developed this uranium

by that I mean capital from a good many countries, not only Canada-the search for uranium went on in the United States and now that they have found great quantities of uranium in that country, when the time comes to renew that contract on which some areas of Canada now depend I hope in Washington they will not point to United States production and say. "No longer do we need your help in this field, thank you very much."
The same problem is arising over oil. The voluntary restrictions that were in effect for a period extending back a couple of years have been replaced by mandatory restrictions. We have some right to complain about that item but we have more right to complain about the reason given for that kind of restriction, that is national security. National security cannot be accepted by Canadians as a valid reason for the imposition of restrictions on continental production. If we are interdependent continentally for defence we ought to be interdependent continentally for the production of oil for defence use in the planes that fly over Canadian territory. Yet we were told that for reasons of national security this cannot be done and our oil imports have to be restricted.
There are other examples. There are increased restrictions placed on our imports as I have mentioned, and increased and unfair competition in marketing abroad our agricultural products, a matter with which all hon. members are familiar. There is also the effect of escape clauses and peril points in the United States reciprocal trade agreement act which minimized the advantages we receive from the legislation. Because of this act and the arrangements made under it at GATT the duties on Canadian exports to the United States in many fields have been considerably reduced in the last ten years. The advantages we have been enjoying from that in the past may now well be threatened by the new escape clauses which the United States can impose against us. Other difficulties are created by the interference with the trade of Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies to areas of the world where it is illegal for a United States company to trade and the effect of United States anti trust


legislation applied to Canadian companies.
I have mentioned only a few illustrations. I do not .think it is an exaggeration when I say that a serious situation has developed in this aspect of our relationship. We must consider what we can do now to prevent that situation deteriorating into economic conflict from which nobody on either side would gain anything. We ask ourselves if the present arrangements in effect are satisfactory to deal with these problems. Are Canadian interests sufficiently considered in the application of the principle of continental interdependence? If not, what can we in this parliament do to improve that situation?
We have, of course, the normal intergovernmental contacts and I suppose they are just as continuous and effective under the present government as they were under the previous government when I can assure hon. gentlemen from personal knowledge they were both close and effective, both personal and official and both formal and informal. We have the use of the diplomatic machinery which I am sure works as effectively now as it has always worked in both Washington and Ottawa. We have some relatively new pieces of machinery and some which go back two or three years.
We have, for example, the intergovernmental cabinet committee on economic matters. It did not meet very often when this party was in office and I would be the last person to say it was a very effective piece of machinery so I am not trying to score any debating points when I say I do not think it is any more effective in its present operations or has met more often in the last year and a half than was the case before 1957. We also have a joint intergovernmental cabinet committee on defence which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) may think is an invaluable piece of machinery but it does not seem to have met very often.
However, we have something new in the joint congressional parliamentary committee which has been set up. This is a piece of machinery that is not only novel in the relationship between the two countries but it could be very important. When I say that I emphasize the word "could" because it could also be almost all window dressing. If that joint congressional parliamentary committee means that every six months there will be a trip to Washington for a couple of days and then in the next six months there will be a trip to Ottawa for a couple of days you would have a good time in Washington and a good time in Ottawa. You would meet opposite numbers in congress and the opposite numbers in parliament. That is all to the good, of course. You would

get to know the problems of Washington and the problems of Ottawa a little better and perhaps that would have some effect, but I do not for one moment believe that a joint committee of this kind, carried on in that way, will have any considerable or lasting effect on the solution of the problems with which we are faced.
I do hope that those who are responsible for the operation of this committee will perhaps discuss together to see whether there is not some way by which this committee, which is of such great potential importance, can be made actually important in the day to day examination which a committee of this kind might make through a permanent staff on both sides, through more frequent business meetings and day to day examination, give to problems which are coming up and which might be considered on this legislative basis before they became a subject of public controversy. I know this is not going to be easy.
One of the difficulties in regard to working out an arrangement of this kind is the difference between our parliamentary and congressional systems. Committees in Washington, as we all know, have an independent, effective existence and indeed an effective influence sometimes on the executive even in spite of the executive. I doubt whether that could be said of committees in a parliamentary system of government. And therefore with this different approach to the parliamentary structure and the functions of committees as they operate under congressional principles it is not going to be easy to work out this new piece of machinery in a way which might help solve this problem of throwing light on them before they become public problems. I hope the government will look at this and see if there is not some way in which this piece of machinery can be made more effective than it will be.
One of the men who has done most to make the United States more aware of the Canadian problems-in that I think we all owe him a debt of gratitude-is Representative Coffin of Maine. Representative Coffin made a speech in Portland, Maine, on February 13. He was dealing with a statement which he had made, when the two congressmen who came up here a few months ago, made a report on the new relations between Canada and the United States which, in his view, perhaps required a new form of association. I know what will be said about that when we approach the United States government, if we approach the United States government, for a new form of association. They will say, what we do for you, you will have to do for others. I say that that argument
Canadian-United. States Relations does not hold water any longer. If in fact our relationship is so important, so intimate, and if this special interdependence between Canada and the United States because of the force of circumstances is not the same as it is between the United States and any other country; if that is the case, perhaps we must ask for some special form of organizational arrangement to reflect that interdependence. Perhaps that is what Representative Coffin had in mind when he said this:
I had come to see that we could expect a reasonable solution of our boundary waters and power problems, our trade differences, our customs and immigration problems, our transportation, agricultural, and fisheries problems only if both congress and the executive were able to take the broad view. On the congressional level this meant giving enough senators and congressmen an understanding of the full range of problems so that in the consideration of any particular measure backed by those with a specific regional or occupational interest, there would be a larger number of legislators who could afford to look at the problem in perspective and strive for a sound approach. On the executive level what is needed is a device or procedure which can bring together the thinking on all of the issues between the two nations. The objective would be to consider some problems en bloc, in a package. For example, one such package proposal is the giving of corridor rights to Canada through the Alaska panhandle in exchange for an agreement as to sharing of benefits from Yukon power development. If all the elements were collected and assessed by the executive branch in an imaginative manner, other combinations might be deemed feasible ways of breaking existing log jams.
I agree with that, so far as I know anything about the United States approach to those problems, but I would go farther. Why not have all those elements collected and assessed by the two governments in the way that Representative Coffin said is becoming essential in the case of the United States? That means, surely, asking for some kind of formal arrangement-I have spoken about this before in this session-some formal treaty arrangement that laid down principles which would guide the conduct of the governments on both sides of the border.
What about the inflexibility of such a plan? I know the hon. gentleman mentioned this before.

I mentioned it before and,
as a matter of fact, the Prime Minister mentioned it. He had something to say about this at page 1550 of Hansard. When he spoke on March 3 he had this to say:
However, we have been speaking of the economic co-operation agreement between Canada and the United States, which is dated October 26, 1950. This document, which all hon. members have,-
This was the document which attempted to prolong the principles of the Hyde Park agreement which governed our relations

Canadian-United States Relations during the war when it was not too difficult to work out relationships of that kind. I continue:
This document, which all hon. members have, sets forth the principles for economic co-operation. The arrangements worked out under the Hyde Park agreement proved so successful that when international conditions again appeared threatening the joint United States-Canada industrial mobilization planning committee was established on April 12, 1949, to make plans in case joint action should again become necessary.
And so on. When we are threatened with some external dangers then we can find ways and means collectively or jointly to deal with those dangers. When that danger disappears we fall back on the old arrangements. Therefore, I suggest that if it was desirable in 1950 to work out a document which laid down certain principles which would govern economic co-operation between the two countries, which was done in a form which was not binding on congress or binding on parliament, and which had no treaty or other legal significance; if it could be done in 1950 in that way, then perhaps the time has come -and I put it no higher than that-to give consideration to the enshrinement of the principle of economic co-operation in a formal treaty arrangement which would be submitted to congress where it could be debated and submitted to parliament where it could be debated. And if the two legislatures agreed we would then have a document which each side could follow in case action was taken by the government of either side which infringed those principles. Perhaps it would be worth while giving consideration to that kind of situation. I think however that we should go farther than that and these are my closing words, I again refer to the speech of Representative Coffin who said:
Beyond this second level of minimizing the Canadian-United States points of contention or friction, to the benefit of both, there lies the ultimate level of Canadian-United States co-operation in policies and programs devised to sparkplug a free world effort to stabilize commodities-
He is right. This approach to the problem is somewhat different. What he had in mind in this speech was to broaden the basis of continental co-operation not only in defence, which I have spoken about, but in the field of trade and economics; broaden the basis so that it will cover the whole of the Atlantic area. The Prime Minister knows my views on this and I know the difficulties in the way of doing any such thing. I used to go to the Atlantic treaty council meetings every spring and every autumn and we used to talk about this kind of thing and it was extremely difficult to do more than talk about it. But perhaps the time has come when we may have to do more than talk about this interest in the alliance because if something


cannot be done to strengthen the non-military basis of the alliance it may fall apart. Indeed, there are some signs of even the military basis of the alliance weakening in the news in the last two or three days. The reason I say this is that there are situations, there are circumstances now which did not exist five years ago and which may perhaps provide more hope, certainly they provide greater opportunity, for progress in this direction than existed a few years ago.
What I am thinking of is the development of the European free trade area, the development of the European common market. Six European countries have now worked out among themselves something that would have been considered absolutely out of the question 15 years ago. If anybody had said that in this or any other legislative chamber before world war II that by 1959 we would have a European economic unit including these European countries it would have been considered as a visionary statement indeed. But we have it now and the other countries of Europe, including Great Britain, are considering whether they can expand this into a European free trade area.
If my hon. friend has been following the debates in the British House of Commons he will know that some very pertinent and significant questions have been asked the government of the United Kingdom as to how they could do this, what would be the effect of joining the European free trade area on commonwealth preferences and all that kind of thing. They are beginning to debate association of the United Kingdom with the European free trade area, and while there is a large gap between debate and action the first steps are being taken. If those steps should lead to a European free trade area with which the North American states, the United States and Canada, have no association at all it will be extremely bad for Canada, both economically and politically, because we will be thrown back on conti-nentalism and we will then learn in a far more vivid way than we know now the effects on our destiny of continental relationships at a time when the Atlantic is split in two between Europe and North America.
Therefore, not only is it of first importance for Canada economically and commercially to do something to widen the basis of freer trade arrangements but perhaps in the long run it is of even greater importance that our political development and political destiny should be brought about not on any continental basis, not even exclusively on a commonwealth basis but by working out in this North Atlantic area closer and closer co-operation with people and countries who think

as we do and who will work with us politically and economically in the face of the menace that confronts us today from countries who do not think like we do.
Before the hon. gentleman goes on, what does he conceive to be the political and economic co-operation that should exist between Canada and these countries of Europe within the free trade area?

I see no reason why we should not now begin, and we would certainly have to try to associate the United States with us, the same kind of consideration in respect of the European free trade area that Great Britain is giving to that area, a consideration of how an association can be brought about which is not based on complete free trade, which does not give up control of separate customs duties but which is based on the development of an area where there will be freer trade between those members than exists at the present time and which perhaps one day will lead to the kind of association you have in a federal state. When I say "one day" I am thinking far into the future. If the Prime Minister thinks this is an imaginative and visionary observation I would ask him and other members of the house whether, in the face of the situation we have in the world today, any other ideal will be enough to safeguard not only our prosperity but also our security.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in view of the considerations I have mentioned I move, seconded by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
this house is of the opinion that recent decisions of the United States government, particularly in the field of production and commercial policy, underline the necessity for the government to make more effective arrangements with the United States to prevent the undesirable impact of those decisions on Canada, and the necessity of a more active participation by the government in working out the implications of interdependence and closer unity within the North Atlantic community.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to express briefly the support of this group for the purpose of the amendment. Before proceeding with my few remarks I must say that we are very pleased indeed to see the official opposition now expressing the same concern over United States influence on defence and trade policies in Canada that this group has been expressing for several years. I think I should once again compliment the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for moving in our direction in this important field. It is another indication of the influence that this small group in the house is having on the somewhat larger group to our left. I hope that influence will continue.
Canadian-United States Relations
We have been very concerned for some years about the impact of United States policies upon Canadian affairs, and this is understandable in view of the greater size of our neighbour to the south. We have been concerned about their influence on external affairs, defence policies, our trade relationships and industry and agriculture in Canada.
To demonstrate the influence that the Americans aim to have on our policies with respect to external affairs I want to use one illustration. We all know that there has been a growing demand in Canada for the recognition of the Peiping government, the mainland government of China. That demand has come not only from the group in this corner of the house but has been made by leading bankers, leading industrialists, particularly in British Columbia, who face the situation realistically, by the Canadian Labour Congress, by the agricultural organizations and by an ever-increasing number of Canadian people who appear to understand the realities of the situation better than the government at the present time. No doubt the growing support in Canada for recognition of the government of the mainland of China is causing some concern to the state department of the United States. I presume that is why Mr. Walter S. Robertson, undersecretary of state for the United States, visited Ottawa a few days ago and addressed a meeting of the Canadian Club in the Chateau Laurier, to which I was very kindly invited. I understand that he also addressed members of thei Progressive Conservative association yesterday and is taking every advantage of his time in Canada to influence Canadian public opinion with respect to this important question.
In that connection I want to quote briefly from an article by Charles Lynch which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on Saturday, March 14. The article is headed, "Why U.S. Won't Recognize Peiping." Mr. Lynch was at the dinner held in the Chateau and this is what he has to say in his article:
One of the most pointed and most important speeches ever made by an official of the United States government in Canada was made here yesterday by Walter S. Robertson, assistant secretary of state for far eastern affairs.
Mr. Robertson is "Mr. China Policy" in the state department.
His speech, before the Canadian club, was as considered and as eloquent a presentation of the U.S. view on communist China as any man could make.
I certainly bear that out because the views of the United States government were very eloquently placed before the meeting by Mr. Robertson.
