The fact that he came to Ottawa to make it is evidence of the concern that is felt in Washington over the trend of Canadian opinion on the Red China question.
A short time ago, the Canadian club heard an eye witness report on communist China by Canadian correspondent Gerald Clark-a hard-hitting, well documented report on the achievements of the Peiping regime.
Mr. Robertson came to present the antidote-not only to the observations of Mr. Clark, but to those of other recent Canadian visitors to mainland China, including James Muir of the Royal Bank of Canada, and Oakley Dalgleish, the publisher of the Toronto Globe and Mail. It is also fair to say that he came to address himself to the Canadian government and its policy of increased trade with communist China.
Then, the article goes on to say in conclusion:
Mr. Robertson's words are unlikely to be echoed from any part of the house in the forthcoming commons debate. But they state, more eloquently than any of our own officials would be ready or willing to do, why the U.S. feels as it does about communist China, and why Canadian policy, as a consequence, continues to be one of non-recognition.
They make clear the size of the breach that would be blown in Canadian-American relations by an Ottawa move toward recognition.
As such, the Robertson speech is an essential backdrop against which the commons debate will be conducted.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is an illustration of the tremendous impact of the government of the United States on this government's foreign policy with respect to the recognition of China. They send Mr. Robertson to Ottawa to address this important meeting and to meet other members of the House of Commons and try to persuade them that United States policy in this respect is correct. However, I am glad to notice, according to this morning's Globe and Mail, that the editor of the Globe and Mail has not been enamoured of Mr. Robertson's remarks. I should like to quote part of this editorial as an antidote to Mr. Robertson's remarks at this time. I think we must give credit to the editor of the Globe and Mail for writing some excellent editorials on foreign policy and other important matters. The final paragraph reads:
Finally, there is Chiang, heading what Mr. Robertson described as "a non-communist Chinese government firmly oriented to the free world". Now, Chiang is certainly non-communist, and he certainly heads a government. But it is not, and has not been for 10 years, a "Chinese" government. It is the government of Formosa, a small island 100 miles off the Chinese coast, which Chiang heads. And he is never going to head anything else. The one and only Chinese government is that at Peking, and neither Chiang nor Mr. Robertson has-if we may coin an expression-a California Republican's chance of overthrowing it.
This is the first thing Canadians must understand in their formulation of an independent, a genuinely Canadian, Far East policy. This is the first point at which Ottawa, as it looks to Asia,
[Mr. Herridge.l
must break with Washington. Chiang is nobody, his rump regime on Formosa means nothing. Canada should immediately disown him.
It will be particularly interesting to note what influence the visit of Mr. Walter Robertson has on the government of Canada in the days to come in connection with its policies with respect to the recognition of this government.
Now, then, the second influence, and a major influence, on Canadian affairs with which this group is seriously concerned is the United States government's influence on our defence policy and all the ramifications which flow from that influence. We have had some lengthy debates on this question in recent days, and I am not going to rehash those debates. We do think in this group that that influence has been increasing at a rapid rate since the signing of the NORAD agreement, this unilateral agreement with respect to the defence of the North American continent. The purpose of the agreement, the defence of the continent, is something with which we are heartily in agreement. However, as we said on the occasion of the debate on the agreement, we in this group object to this unilateral approach to defence which places Canada at an increasing disadvantage with respect to the defence policy of the United States and the United States at an increasing advantage.
On that occasion we urged that defence policy should be based, first, on the United Nations, and urged the strengthening of the international police force and the conception that goes behind that international police force. Secondly, we claimed that the defence of the North American continent should be part of the duties of NATO and that NORAD should be an integral part of NATO. In that connection, I want once again to congratulate the leader of the official opposition. I think in recent days, although I have heard him mention it before, he has been coming more and more to the C.C.F. point of view, because during the debate on the NORAD agreement there was not a word from the Liberal benches-
Oh, yes.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman has forgotten, but I have, from the very beginning, advocated that NORAD should be part of the NATO command.
I sincerely apologize.
Perhaps the hon. member forgets the amendment which he introduced was ruled out of order before anybody had a chance to speak on it.

I apologize if I was incorrect in that statement. I certainly accept the word of the Leader of the Opposition in this

respect. Perhaps I should say that there has been an increasing emphasis then, and that is possibly why I have noticed it in recent days, on this aspect of their policy which we are pleased to see.
I come now in my few brief remarks to the question of agricultural policies and industrial policies. Agricultural policies of the United States, particularly their disposal programs, have had a very serious effect upon the wellbeing of the farmers of this country, particularly the farmers of western Canada. Possibly if these policies had not been given effect the large delegation that visited Ottawa last week would not have had the same reason to visit Ottawa and would not be suffering the same distress. In any event, I am not going into that because the matter has been dealt with much more effectively than I could do so by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). Perhaps I am a little premature in that statement. He has a thorough knowledge of the circumstances of the grain producers.
I want to add a few words with respect to the impact on Canadian industry of United States policies, particularly with respect to the control of United States subsidiaries in Canada. This subject has been mentioned in this house on a number of occasions. There was the cancellation of the order for trucks that was given by some representative or agency of the government of Peking; the cancellation of the order for aluminum under the direction of the parent company in the United States; the cancellation of the order for certain rubber products from the Goodyear tire people on instructions of the parent company in the United States. We in this group, Mr. Speaker, think it is an intolerable situation that a company operating in Canada should be subject to control of the laws of the government of the United States. If companies come to this country to operate and to reap their profits we in this group say those companies should be willing to abide by Canadian law and operate first to the advantage of the Canadian people.
In following my argument, I should like to quote briefly from the Gordon commission report. I should say that the Gordon commission discovered the reason for Canadian anxiety about foreign investment, and I quote from page 390 of the final report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects as follows:
At the root of Canadian concern about foreign investment is undoubtedly a basic, traditional sense of insecurity vis-4-vis our friendly, albeit our much larger and more powerful neighbour, the United States. There is concern that as the position of American capital in the dynamic resource and manufacturing sectors becomes ever more dominant, our economy will inevitably become more
Canadian-United. States Relations and more integrated with that of the United States. Behind this is the fear that continuing integration might lead to economic domination by the United States and eventually to the loss of our political independence.
That is what a great number of Canadians fear at this time,
This fear of domination by the United States affects to some extent the political climate of life in Canada today. Therefore it is a factor which has some bearing upon "the probable economic development of Canada and the problems to which such development appears likely to give rise".
The Gordon commission report notes that many Canadians are worried over the fact that such a large degree of economic decision making is in the hands of non-residents, particularly United States citizens. In that connection the report has this to say at page 389:
This concern has arisen because of the concentration of foreign ownership in certain industries, because of the fact that most of it is centred in one country, the United States, and because most of it is in the form of equities which, in the ordinary course of events, are never likely to be repatriated.
The next aspect of this problem which is also of great importance is the fact that a very large part of United States equity investment in Canada is in the form of "wholly-owned" subsidiaries and branches of United States parent corporations. This means that although such companies virtually control important sections of the Canadian economy, it is absolutely impossible for Canadians to purchase ownership in them. This situation has been the cause of protest across this country. If a Canadian wishes to buy into Canadian General Motors, for example, he must buy shares in the United States parent corporation. This means that his Canadian investment is in the entire operation of General Motors conducted in the United States and elsewhere as well as in Canada. Thus there is no Canadian investment as such. It is even possible for a Canadian to invest in one of these parent companies and lose on his investment, despite the fact that the Canadian subsidiary may be showing a substantial profit.
I might say that I have had residents in my own constituency write to me in that connection, people who were interested in the lumber industry and in the pulp and paper industry and who wanted to purchase shares in a subsidiary of the Celanese Corporation of America which operates a large forest management operation under licence, partly in my constituency. They were not allowed to do so. They were obliged to buy shares in the parent company. Other residents in my district own shares in a certain relatively small British Columbia lumber company, I think it is Canadian Western. This company has been absorbed by a United

Canadian-United. States Relations States company. Therefore their shares are included in the shares of the parent company in the United States. The very thing which they thought they were doing, namely investing in a Canadian industry, or the very thing they invested their money for has now changed its complexion.
There may be a conflict of interests, that is to say, the best interests of Canada may not at all be the same as the best interests of shareholders of a foreign parent company controlling the policies of subsidiaries in Canada. To illustrate how a clash of interests may take place, I want to quote again from the Gordon commission report which cites the oil industry as an example:
-in the oil industry the same large international companies, or their affiliates and subsidiaries, which broadly speaking dominate the producing, refining and marketing sections of the Canadian industry, are the principal suppliers of crude oil to the large market centred in Montreal, and are important suppliers in most areas of the United States. The immediate and continuing interest of the Canadian subsidiaries of these companies, and indeed of Canada, is to find increasing markets for Canadian oil in the United States, or. failing that, perhaps in the Montreal area. Without growing markets a large part of the oil being discovered in western Canada would have to be "shut in" perhaps for some considerable period. The importance and the immediacy of this problem of markets for the oil industry in Canada is clear enough to Canadians. Quite understandably, it may appear somewhat less important and less immediate to those in other countries who control the situation and who have world-wide interests to consider.
I think that is another good illustration of the effect which the policy of parent companies in the United States has on the development of Canadian national resources.
In concluding my brief remarks on this question, I want to suggest that some recommendations made by the Gordon commission could be very well incorporated in legislation and be introduced by this government. The commission recommends that subsidiaries of foreign-owned corporations should be compelled to:
1.	Sell an appreciable interest-approximately 25 per cent-in their equity stock to Canadians. In order to ensure that the 25 per cent would not revert to United States ownership, such shares would have to be made transferable only to Canadians or residents of Canada. Another method would be to provide that such shares would lose their voting rights on transfer to non-Canadians.
2.	Include on the board of directors a number of independent Canadians.
3.	Employ wherever possible a certain number of Canadians in senior management and technical positions.
4.	Publish their financial statements, and make full disclosure of their Canadian operations.
Furthermore, we believe that legislation should be enacted to prevent the passing of control or ownership of Canadian banks and insurance companies into foreign hands by providing that shares in such institutions which in the future are acquired by nonresidents of Canada be ineligible to vote.
Is the hon. gentleman not aware of the fact that last year we passed some legislation to prevent the transfer of insurance companies to the United States?

Yes; I am fully aware of that fact but it does not cover the complete picture as would the recommendations.
We in this group would like to see the government of Canada introduce legislation to implement the remedies suggested in the Gordon commission report. While those recommendations would not meet the situation completely, from our point of view it would at least indicate that this government was taking a step in the direction that it has advocated, and which some of its members have advocated vociferously in this house when in opposition.
I was very much interested in the suggestion made by the leader of the official opposition, namely that consideration might be given, if I understood him correctly, to a trade treaty between the United States and Canada. We in this group think that suggestion merits close consideration. It would provide an opportunity for representatives of this government to go into every aspect of business that arises in the circumstances that we have mentioned and others and would codify in a sense and be a means of reaching an agreement that I think would be the commencement of laying the foundation of much sounder trading relationships in the future.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I must say that we in this group were pleased to see the leader of the official opposition introduce this subject by his amendment into the house today. It is an important question. It concerns a large number of Canadians. As the result of the introduction of this amendment and any other amendments or subamendments that may be introduced I trust that the government will be influenced to start walking in the direction in which it has urged others to walk in the years passed, namely in the direction of Canada's interests with respect to external affairs, foreign policy, defence policy, agricultural policy and industrial policy.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for the introduction of the amendment, but nevertheless I do welcome the opportunity

to express a few opinions in relation to two aspects of the subject with which the resolution deals. As the Leader of the Opposition mentioned in his initial remarks, this is one of those opportunities when the opposition has the right to criticize the government and government policy; but after listening to him, I rather had the feeling that he really was not very annoyed with us. The very nature of the amendment itself, phrased in such broad generalities, reminded me so much of that old adage which is attributed to people who have been in political office for some time, "We must never build our political fences so high that they cannot adequately be straddled at all times."
I felt this was the nature of the comments which the Leader of the Opposition made, for while in these loose generalities he suggested that we should make some improvements, or some more effective general arrangements-he made a reference to the possibility of establishing a treaty-I think it can be adequately pointed out that the long range program aimed at improving the understanding between our two countries has to a very substantial measure alleviated a situation which certainly could have been considerably worse had some action not been taken. I propose to itemize these aspects in my brief remarks this afternoon.
Every member of this house is naturally concerned with the problem of our relationships with other countries, in particular with the United States. I rather feel, Mr. Speaker, that I have some particular interest in that matter, because in the consular area of my own constituency there are some 46,000 Americans. I think we have set an example to the rest of Canada, and certainly to the rest of the world, of how good neighbours can exist side by side in the working out of many domestic problems and, yes, of many national problems.
Let us look at the history of our problems very briefly. The long standing complaint, of course, by Canadians has been that we for the most part have been ignored by the United States. I suggest that the action of the United States congress in the past year, associated with the economic life of that country, has to a very substantial degree alleviated and reduced, in fact almost eliminated the argument that we have been ignored. There are four very obvious examples of that. First of all, the visit of the President of the United States to this house of parliament. Second, there was the extension of the reciprocal trade act. Third, there was the production of the Hays-Coffin report which has already been referred to; and fourth, there was the acceptance by
Canadian-United States Relations United States congress of the need of a joint legislative committee between our two countries.
I was not in a position to thoroughly understand whether the Leader of the Opposition approved or disapproved of the establishment of this committee. I think in effect what he did question was its effectiveness. I suggest to you, sir, that the first advantage to be gained from this committee and its appointment has already been accomplished. At long last we have some body which can deal effectively to define the area where our disagreement actually lies. So often we hear individuals on both sides of the border complaining about certain frictions which they insist exist.
Then when you examine them you find that many are actually imaginary. So I believe that the Canada-United States committee has, by its very appointment and through the work it has in front of it, the opportunity to define the area of disagreement, and once that has been accomplished it can bring back its report to the two legislative bodies they respectively represent. There we can see some attempt to reconcile the differences wherever they may exist.
I propose to deal with two of those difficulties. The first, which has been introduced many times into the house since March 10, is the question of the United States imposition of mandatory controls on the importation of Canadian oil. The history of this particular problem is one which has its basis of fact in that area of the United States which in past years had become oil deficient or short of oil is now in a surplus position. Then in June of 1957 we saw the introduction, first, of the voluntary controls which were later amended and made somewhat more severe. Then secondly, and more recently, as a result of the justice department of the United States advising the United States government that mandatory controls were essential because the voluntary controls offended the United States anti trust act, we saw the imposition of controls providing restriction to a greater degree than we have ever experienced before.
I think the first point that should be made, is that these controls were directed against all foreign importers. They were designed primarily against the largest importers of oil into the United States, the Venezuelan and Middle East countries bloc. The President and the United States government have said that they were designed to have least effect on Canada, and I think to a degree it can be said that there is some truth to this in that certain exemptions were made in the marketing area in the United States into which the Saskatchewan crude flows. But no one will

States Relations disagree with the argument offered by the Leader of the Opposition that this was indeed a slap in the face to Canada, certainly based on the argument that in the interests of continental defence the United States could not declare our country exempt from the restrictions imposed on the other countries. I suggest that the real basis of the United States action was not the question of continental defence or the maintaining of a healthy petroleum industry, but was rather that the United States government succumbed to the very large and effective oil lobby which exists in Washington.
The problem we have, however-and let us look at the future-is that while Canada, it is true, was unable under certain circumstances to take advantage of the full quotas, it is certainly a wrong impression for anyone to suggest that these quotas were not harmful. Actually the restriction had this effect on us: We found that the market area of the United States was reduced. The net result was that the effect of competition had a very serious effect in particular on the markets which we refer to as district No. 5, the Pacific northwest of the United States, because all other foreign importers began to concentrate on the availability of the quotas open to all countries. In such a circumstance the Canadian found that he could not compete with the low concessional oil which, in many instances, was produced anywhere from 14 cents to 25 cents a barrel, compared with oil in Canada which would average $1 to $1.10 per barrel. So during the past year we as a country, because of the voluntary, now mandatory, restriction, reduced our imports into the United States by better than 40 per cent. Fortunately the domestic demand, particularly in Ontario, maintained a reasonably healthy oil situation, but the industry has been able to produce only about 50 per cent of its capacity compared with the United States average of 75 per cent.
Let us look at the action that has taken place. As I mentioned, these quotas were imposed on all importers. On several occasions Canada made representations to the United States government pointing out that in the interests of continental defence and our general trading relationships we should be declared exempt, first of all because we are separated only by a pipeline and not a waterway. In addition to this the report prepared by Messrs. Hays and Coffin which pointed out there should be no difference between the oil produced in Texas and the oil produced in Alberta in the interests of defence. The many important groups and bodies within the United States in addition to those in Canada that have asked the United

States government to give consideration to the Canadian people in this respect have all been ignored. Today we find ourselves in a situation where if the door has not been completely closed to us it has most certainly to a large extent been shut.
We should remember that this restrictive action began as early as May or June of 1957 because of the building up of the surplus supply of oil in the United States that started immediately following the Suez crisis. After representations made to the United States government were turned down Canada was required to develop other markets within its own borders. As I mentioned, Ontario fortunately took up part of the demand. We now find ourselves on the horns of a dilemma. On the one hand we have been told that these quotas are essential in order to maintain a healthy industry in the United States and on the other hand our application for exemption was rejected. We cannot be declared exempt because we lack a continental agreement.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke today of the need to make more effective arrangements on the basis of some treaty. This is by no means a new idea. The greatest obstacle in this proposal would be endeavouring to spell out in an agreement arrangements in relation to an industry such as the oil and gas industry. Let us bear in mind that voluntary oil import quotas represent only one aspect of the problem of this industry and our relationship to the United States in this field. In many instances the United States federal power commission has failed to co-operate with Canadian interests. Licences have been granted to Canadian exporters in the past by the Canadian government; however, if I may use the term, we in Canada have had the short end of the stick in that the federal power commission has failed to act. With respect to this aspect of the problem it is understandable that the Canadian government has adopted a firm attitude prior to granting any export licence for gas and I suggest that now is the time for even firmer action to be taken with respect to oil.
We have seen the building up of reserves of oil in the United States which have prevented our marketing our products in that country. We have seen little likelihood as a result of the presidential statement of any hope for a change in this policy although the press release made a loose reference to future defence arrangements to be worked out between Venezuela, Canada and the United States. If the Canadian government is not in a position to negotiate a general agreement on a top level basis with the two

countries to which I referred surely this government must adopt a policy that will tend to sell more oil to Canadians.
I believe, in other words, we have reached the time when a quota system in Canada should be seriously considered. This is not a means of retaliation; rather, it is merely a matter of adjusting our own economy to make absolutely certain that we provide the required markets for Canadian producers. This is not a criticism of any policy that has been introduced up to this point. There was every reason to follow the policy of retaining the most economic markets in the United States, especially that of district No. 5 in the Pacific northwest. It is wrong for us to endeavour to obtain markets that are many miles distant only if we are unable to work out some arrangement with the United States.
I suggest, therefore, that now is the time to introduce legislation of our own in this field as a protection to Canadians, although this government through no fault of its own, has nevertheless been unsuccessful in persuading the government of the United States to change its policy. It will not be easy to work out arrangements under which the United States market may be retained. We have frequently been told by the United States that if we could satisfy Venezuela in terms of persuading that country that our being exempted from United States restrictions would not affect them we would better be able to negotiate an agreement with the United States. The complications involved in working out any agreement render it a near impossibility. I therefore believe it is time that we developed our own markets and examined how we might introduce policies to adequately deal with the situation.
I wish to speak for a moment about investment capital. The Leader of the Opposition suggested that we should not become completely reliant upon this for the development of our country. This is an obvious statement we all accept. May I urge, however, that in our desire to judge fairly whether or not this capital has been dangerous in terms of its volume putting us in the position of being subject to United States dominance and in generally assessing its effect on the economy, let us not discourage United States capital from coming into Canada. Let us examine the history of what it has produced for us. The oil industry which requires over $1 million a day to operate could never have developed to its present stage without the assistance of United States capital. We do not generate enough capital in Canada to take care of the demands of this industry alone.
Canadian-United States Relations We could also consider the development of our mining industry and the pulp and paper industry. To a substantial degree these have been assisted by United States investment.
I suggest that we have all the legislation and lawmakers we require to ensure that the rights of Canadians are protected which is of course essential but if we do anything to discourage the flow of United States capital into Canada we will regret it for many years to come, for it will affect the orderly progress and development of our country. We should not forget that we have also attracted European capital to Canada.
I fail to understand those people who on the one hand criticize the advantages to be gained by having United States investment capital in Canada and on the other indicate concern about the lack of progress and development of Canadian industries. I believe it is fair to say that during the past year the oil and gas industry led the boom in this country in its period of prosperity and progress. If we do anything to discourage investment capital it will retard our expansion and reduce the level of prosperity we are enjoying today.
We should bear in mind that this capital is employed in a variety of industries producing new wealth and higher standards of living for Canadians and therefore we cannot be concerned with the nationality of the dollar that serves us so well. Instead we should lay ground rules so the dollar can be employed in Canada's development, and in Canada's interest.
The majority of United States companies in the petroleum industry already recognize the above fact. Many insist on employing Canadian management and staff in their subsidiaries. Many are taking an active part in the community life of Canadian cities and many invite Canadian participation in their new underwritings. Through their affiliates and subsidiaries in the development of the by-products of the industry these companies have generated vast wealth for the benefit of Canadians.
Finally, may I say, Mr. Speaker, to the Leader of the Opposition that when we enter into a debate which on the one hand suggests that the rights and the sovereignty of our country are at stake and in jeopardy we must also assume the responsibility of recognizing that to a very large degree we have obtained the level of development which we have today because of the co-operative attitude we have worked out with the United States. On the other hand, it is not inconsistent to say to the United States, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has said on a number of

Canadian-United States Relations occasions, that we as Canadians will insist on our rights. We recognize that there are disagreements between us. These, however, are not insurmountable. They may be worked out on a basis of common understanding.
I take pride in the fact that in Canada we have developed a growing nationalism, a nationalism which has for the first time in many years made Canadians realize that we have a common bond-that we are not poor relations in the family of world nations. I think it is a very sound thing that we have developed an appreciation of what we own, and the assets that we have, within our borders. I think however that it would be a sad day if in the building up of any animosities-because to a large degree many are purely imaginary-we were to do anything which would destroy a relationship between our two countries which has been second to none. I suggest that if we did that we would be doing a disservice to the people of Canada.
I suppose it will be said of me, as one who is concerned more than any other in this house with the problems of this one industry, that this is being inconsistent. This is not the case at all, Mr. Speaker. I have stated very clearly that because of the position in which the petroleum industry is now in, a mineral industry which is the No. 1 industry in Canada and so important to the welfare of the entire dominion, it is necessary for us to take our own action in the interest of Canadians. If we do that the United States administration will be the first to appreciate not only our right but the need for such action. Therefore, in speaking to this admendment I suggest that it is very difficult on the one hand to talk about the great concern which we have about the encroachment on our sovereignty and on the other to accept the benefits that we have obtained by the building up of a great nation in this country which to a large degree has resulted from the cooperative attitude which has been taken in that one country of all the countries of the world.

Mr. Speaker, the subject of the discussion is perhaps one which affects the lives of more people than any other topic, which cannot be treated lightly and upon which there should be a broad area of agreement in all parties.
One of the greatest factors in international relations is the problem of mutual understanding between the citizens of neighbouring nations such as Canada and the United States. Happily, there exists a community of interest between those two nations which is rather unique in the world today, a community of interest which provides the greatest


opportunity for the exemplification of international understanding and good will. For that understanding to deteriorate would be a sad blow to both countries as well as a sad blow to the other free nations of the world.
One of the world's greatest needs today is understanding and good will in the international field. These two nations, Canada and the United States, are very fortunate to have the opportunity to demonstrate to the world how to get along together even in the face of some conflict of interest. Understanding, friendship and good will must remain as solid as the rock of Gibraltar between those two nations, but unless we work steadily and constructively for this development the rock will give way and misunderstanding will set in. However, in our dealings with our powerful neighbour, while always friendly, we must also be firm whenever our interests are in serious jeopardy, caused by some contemplated action of the United States.
Apart from the delicate relationship of mutual defence and recurring irritations about mutual trade, there is one other very serious problem which concerns my own constituency in a very particular way and it concerns every municipality along the St. Lawrence seaway. I am speaking of the diversion of water from lake Michigan by the city of Chicago which in effect will threaten the water levels of the great lakes, thus affecting navigation along the St. Lawrence seaway and most certainly the new projected seaway terminal at the lakehead. What worries the people of the lakehead and elsewhere is the feeble protest of our government, if it can be called a protest, against this new attempt of water stealing by the city of Chicago.
The supreme court of the United States issued a decree which provided that after December 31, 1958 the diversion of water from lake Michigan through the Chicago canal should be limited to 1,500 cubic feet of water per second. However, the city of Chicago is now trying to increase the diversion permitted by an additional 1,000 cubic feet of water per second. In spite of the fact that a bill to permit this addition was blocked in the United States, senate in 1958, the demand by the city of Chicago is on again and with added vigour.
The bill was passed.

No, the bill is not passed. Only a few days ago the mayor of Chicago made a statement to the effect that the diversion of water from lake Michigan was none of Canada's business. I submit that

this is very much our business and the mayor of Chicago should know better than to make such a statement, unbecoming to the office which he holds; but perhaps it may be that he is preparing himself for an election. As a matter of fact, I understand there is an election going on now in the city of Chicago.
It is generally admitted that the lowering of the levels of lake Huron and lake Erie would handicap the seaway project, which is Canada's business and Fort William and Port Arthur-in fact all of northwestern Ontario

would be directly affected and indirectly even the interests of the prairie provinces would feel the impact by injury to the shipping route.
Today I received a letter from the city clerk of the corporation of the city of Fort William which illustrates the deep concern of our city in this matter of diversion and I now wish to read it to the house:
I am directed to advise you that at a meeting of the council of the corporation of the city of Fort William held on the 10th instant, the following resolution of its finance committee was unanimously adopted, a copy of which I was instructed to forward you for your consideration:
"That whereas the metropolitan sanitary district of greater Chicago in the United States of America is contemplating the further diversion of water from lake Michigan for its sewage disposal systems;
And whereas this diversion of water is detrimental to the harbour development of the city of Fort William;
Be it therefore resolved that representations be made to the federal government to protest the action of the Chicago authority and to halt the unwarranted diversion of water by the metropolitan sanitary district of greater Chicago;
And that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the Prime Minister of Canada, the Ontario water resources commission of Ontario, and to Mr. H. Badanai, M.P., and to Mr. Clare E. Mapledoram, M.L.A., for Fort William."
The suggestion has also been made that the city of Chicago is interested in the diversion for the purpose of developing hydro power in that area. If that is true, Mr. Speaker, this matter is even more serious than it appeared to be at first. According to the records, when the Prime Minister and his supporters were in opposition they were loud in condemning the Liberal government for not speaking loudly enough to the United States in the protection of Canada's interests. But the question now is, is the government doing anything about them?
What has been the attitude of the government since it came into power with respect to the present water diversion? Some of the answers can be found in Hansard. On August 2, 1958, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) gave the following answer to a question put to him by the hon. member
Canadian-United States Relations for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy). I quote from page 3009 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to answer the question which was addressed to me on Wednesday, July 30, by the hon. member for Lambton West dealing with water diversion at Chicago. My answer to his question, which was directed to three main points, is as follows:
1.	The position taken by Canada with respect to a proposed additional diversion of 1,000 cubic feet per second from lake Michigan at Chicago is set forth in an aide memoire dated January 6, 1958. As the document is somewhat long, I ask leave to have it printed as an annex to Hansard.
2.	To the extent that any additional diversion of water may take place at Chicago, the level of the lower lakes and connecting channels will be reduced as far as Montreal, and there will be a corresponding reduction in the availability of water for hydroelectric generation at Niagara, Barnhart and Beauharnois. The effect, however, varies at different places and at different times over a period of years. I should be pleased to arrange for the hon. member to consult tables and graphs in order to determine precisely what effect a particular diversion would have at a specific time in a specific place.
3.	Principles applicable to a diversion from lake Michigan would not necessarily apply to boundary waters, as lake Michigan is not a boundary water.
I think I should perhaps read the aide memoire because it is very important to understand exactly what we are talking about. The aide memoire alluded to by the Secretary of State for External Affairs is headed, "Chicago Diversion-Aide Memoire from Canada to United States", and reads as follows:
Useful conversations between United States and Canadian officials were held in Ottawa on July 7, 1957 on the subject of the sanitation problems which gave rise to proposed legislation for a three-year temporary diversion of 1,000 cubic feet of water per second from the great lakes system and on the subject of studies to be carried out under the proposed legislation.
The Canadian government understands that if such legislation is enacted these sanitation studies will not be limited to evaluating the effects of dilution but will also include consideration of all possible measures for dealing with waste disposal facilities at Chicago. Such measures would include:
(a)	complete separation of storm sewers from the domestic sewerage system or expansion of the existing treatment facilities to serve a total combined flow;
(b)	treatment of organic wastes in industrial plants before discharging these effluents into the sewerage system;
(c)	chlorination of effluent before discharge into the Illinois waterway; and
(d)	artificial aeration of the waterway.
The treatment of sewage in the Chicago area is, of course, a matter entirely within the jurisdiction of the competent legislative bodies within the United States. It is understood that present treatment of waste represents a vast improvement over conditions which existed in former years and that under the present day uses of the water the waste is more a nuisance than a menace to the public health in the area.
In considering the economics of alternative methods of improved waste disposal, it is assumed that full consideration will be given to the economic harm which may be done to navigation and

Canadian-United States Relations hydroelectric generation in both countries by extended use of dilution methods.
It is not possible to give a firm undertaking to provide flows of a particular volume through the existing Longlac and Ogoki diversions to the great lakes basin during the three-year period envisaged by proposed United States legislation. However, if it were possible to offset part of the effects of the Chicago diversion by inflows from the Albany basin in Canada, it would be equitable that an equivalent amount of water should remain available for use in hydroelectric power generation by the Ontario interests at St. Marys falls, Niagara falls and in the international section of the St. Lawrence river until the effects of the proposed temporary diversion will have ceased to be felt in the great lakes system.
All rights under the provisions of the boundary waters treaty of 1909 are specifically reserved.
That is the aide memoire from the Canadian embassy in Washington, dated January 6, 1958. As found on page 620 of Hansard for February 3, 1959, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) asked this question:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I should like to know whether the government has sent a note of protest to the United States government in connections with Bill HR-1 now before congress for the further diversion of water out of the great lakes into the Chicago drainage canal.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs replied:
Mr. Speaker, as I informed the house a few days ago this matter relating to the purport of Bill HR-1 is under consideration. We are considering various representations that have been made by officials and by other organizations. We have not made a protest.
As late as February 12 the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) asked the following question, as found at page 946 of Hansard:
Has the minister yet sent a protest on behalf of this government to the United States government? If not, does he realize that he has only a week left before the hearings begin in the senate on this matter?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs replied:
As I informed the house on two recent occasions, this matter is under close study by our officials and, as I indicated a moment ago, we are ready and anxious to get information with respect to the discussions. We do realize that the hearings will begin in the near future, but that does not indicate that the bill then will be adopted.
Now, Mr. Speaker, after studying the answers to the questions asked on the subject, one cannot help but come to the conclusion that the indication of softness in the Canadian aide memoire must have created the impression in Washington that all was well and that Chicago could go ahead with its plans for diversion.
At a convention of the lake carriers' association of the United States and the dominion marine association, held in Ottawa last January, a resolution was passed unanimously

opposing the diversion of water from the great lakes watershed. I wish to read that resolution:
Whereas, the several states and provinces bordering on the great lakes hold title to those waters under a high public trust to protect and preserve them for the benefit of all their citizens; and
Whereas, by the Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909, the United States and Canada have dedicated the waters of the great lakes to the primary purpose of commerce and navigation to be enjoyed by their citizens, subject only to certain uses by riparian states and provinces not inconsistent with such primary purpose; and
Whereas, by the law common to the United States and Canada any diversion of such waters by any riparian or other user constitutes a wrong against all other riparian owners; and
Whereas, any diversion of water from lake Michigan lowers the natural level of that lake and lakes Huron, Erie, Ontario, their connecting and tributary waters and the St. Lawrence river; directly impairs the natural depth of rivers and harbours, nullifies improvements therein, reduces the carrying capacity of Canadian and the United States great lakes fleets and increases transportation costs, all to the detriment and injury of the people; and
Whereas, the waterborne commerce of the great lakes is indispensable to the growth and wellbeing of the United States and Canada; and
Whereas, any diversion in one country gives rise to dispute between the people of that country and the people of the other country, which should in the interests of their friendly relations be referred for investigation and recommendation as to solution to some tribunal in which the people of the two countries have equal voice:
Now, therefore, be it resolved that the dominion marine association and lake carriers' association, in joint meeting assembled at Ottawa, Ontario, Canada, this 26th day of January 1959, do hereby express their unalterable opposition to any diversion of water from the great lakes watershed and urge that the Congress of the United States refrain from passing legislation authorizing any diversion of water from the great lakes, which diversion would violate solemn treaty rights and obligations between the two nations and would pillage the natural resources of the great lakes watershed vested by law and by decision of the Supreme Court of the United States in the people of the great lakes basin; and
Be it further resolved that the two associations hereby urge that the United States and Canada refer to the international joint commission all questions concerning the diversion of water from the great lakes for full investigation and recommendation as to solution to the end that all controversies may be laid at rest and the rights of the people of the great lakes watershed be preserved; and
Be it further resolved that a copy of this resolution be furnished to the chief executive of the respective national governments of the two countries and to each governor or prime minister, as the case may be, of states and provinces bordering on the great lakes and St. Lawrence river.
Those people who are saying that there is no cause for alarm should ponder over the meaning of some editorials which appeared in the Chicago Tribune, one in February, 1957 and the other in February, 1959. As an

illustration of the seriousness of this matter, I should like to quote from the editorial of February, 1957, which says:
Twice President Eisenhower has vetoed bills permitting a slight increase in lake diversion at Chicago. In the second veto message last August 9 he said he believed no increase should be granted without negotiation with Canada, and he announced that he had asked the state department to undertake discussions with that country.
We said at the time that such parleys were unnecessary, since neither congress nor the supreme court has recognized that Canada has any legal right to interfere with diversion from lake Michigan. Now it appears that the state department has not bothered itself to carry out the president's directive.
Members of the Canadian parliament who recently sought to get their government's views on the matter were told that no consultation had been requested by the United States. The questioners were referred to the terms of the 1909 boundary waters treaty which says that each government reserves to itself-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member is reading a comment upon what has taken place in the house, which strictly is not in accordance with the practice. As I understand what he is reading, it refers to what has already been done earlier this session.

I am speaking on the contemplated water diversion from the great lakes at Chicago. This has a direct bearing on the relations between Canada and the United States, and that is why I am taking the liberty of reading this portion of the editorial.
The Canadian government might have added, for further clarification, that the treaty was made when the diversion rate was assumed to be 10,000 cubic feet a second, and the agreement specifically provided that its terms did not apply to "cases already existing", which included the diversion rate at Chicago.
Now the rate is fixed by a supreme court decision at only 1,500 cubic feet a second. The bills vetoed by the president would have increased the rate to 2,500 cubic feet for a three-year experimental period during which army engineers would study the effects.
We have no objections to the failure of the state department to negotiate with Canada. Perhaps the department has at last discovered that the question is one for congress to decide and that Canada's opinion is irrelevant. If so, President Eisenhower ought to be advised by the department. The bill for increased diversion then can be passed promptly by congress and there will be no excuse for another veto.
Then, I should like to quote a few paragraphs from this other editorial which appeared in the same newspaper in February, 1959.
If Chicago is "stealing" water, it is doing so by order of the United States supreme court and by an act of congress authorizing the diverted water to be used for navigation in the Illinois waterway. The matter of how much water is needed for navigation in the waterway has never been decided, but the supreme court has ruled that congress has the power to fix that amount.

The army engineers say that permanent regulation of the lake levels to prevent the cyclical changes would present no great engineering difficulties. Illinois would be glad to take part in such a program and to pay its share of the cost. The other lake states would do the same, abandoning their false propaganda and mischievous litigation, if they really wished to stabilize lake levels.
That is the end of the quotation from that editorial. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) speaking to the Canadian club at Montreal on December 9, 1957, had this to say about our water resources and I shall quote just a few paragraphs:
The importance of water conservation is growing along with the nation. It must consist of more than a response to immediate emergencies such as floods or water shortages as it has too often been in the past. The conservation of water, as indeed of any natural resource, looks to both the present and the future; it is this characteristic which gives it special significance. In seeing to it that our resources are used wisely and well we recognize that, however important they may be to us today, they have a still greater role to play. Meeting the problems of conserving our water resources is both a challenge and an opportunity measured by the contribution which these resources can make to Canada's future development.
The minister is to be congratulated for pointing out the challenge for the conservation not only of our water resources but also of our rights whenever and wherever they may contested. I respectfully submit that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, for whom I have great respect, or the Prime Minister should give the house a clear statement without any equivocation as to what action the government contemplates taking to safeguard our interest in the great lakes.

Mr. Speaker, the remarks of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) with regard to the Chicago diversion have already been dealt with in advance by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) and I think there is no need to refer to that question at this time. I should like to refer, however, to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) which were confused as to the present, bemused as to the future and apparently forgetful of the past. The amendment he moved was in these terms:
This house is of the opinion that recent decisions of the United States government, particularly in the field of production and commercial policy, underline the necessity for the government to make more effective arrangements with the United States to prevent the undesirable impact of those decisions on Canada, and the necessity of a more active participation by the government in working out the implications of interdependence and closer unity within the North Atlantic community.
We must wonder at once just what he has in mind when he mentions the North Atlantic

Canadian-United States Relations community. Is he referring to the nations of the NATO alliance or has he in mind some wider group of nations? Is he referring to that great trading area upon which the nations of the North Atlantic depend for trade but which by no means is restricted solely the nations of the North Atlantic? The trading area of the nations of the North Atlantic goes far beyond that ocean. That area depends for its trade on the Far East and the Middle East as well as other parts of the world. This amendment, I submit, is confused in that particular.
I should like to deal for a moment with the proposal he made as to the future relations between this country and the United States. This proposal is similar to the one he made in the House of Commons on February 26, when, as reported at page 1410 of Hansard, he said:
I have been wondering whether the time has not now come for a top level formal conference between the leaders in Canada and the United States to see if some formal agreement could not be reached and embodied in a formal convention, perhaps for ratification by legislatures-because this would be one way of bringing these matters to the attention of congress as well as parliament-embodying principles that should govern our relations.
On that occasion, when I rose to speak, as reported at page 1435 of Hansard, I said:
The Leader of the Opposition mentioned at some length a suggestion with regard to the formulation of a new group-a formal conference, I believe he called it-to deal with problems relating to the United States.
The Leader of the Opposition rose at that time and said this:
On a point of order, I wish the hon. member would explain what he means, because I made no such suggestions, nothing remotely approaching it.
By reference to Hansard we can see now that is exactly what he was proposing then and that is exactly what he is proposing now.
One of the difficulties raised in connection with this question-which the Leader of the Opposition has raised at this time and which I dealt with on February 26-is the very nature of the difference between our two governments. May I refer for a moment to the terms of the exchange of notes that was made between Canada and the United States on October 26, 1950, a document to which he has referred, which clearly illustrates the limitations of this sort of agreement. The note reads:
In the Interests of mutual security and to assist both governments to discharge their obligations under the United Nations charter and the North Atlantic Treaty, it is believed that this field of common action should be further extended. It is agreed, therefore, that our two governments shall co-operate in all respects practicable, and to the extent of their respective executive powers-

I emphasize that particular point, because of course the executive powers of the government of the United States are different from the powers of the government of Canada. The executive powers of the United States, under their system of government, are restricted. To make such an agreement binding in fact on our two countries the restriction would require, as I said on February 26, a self-denying ordinance on the part of the House of Representatives and the Senate of the United States, denying them the right to deal with these matters of international obligations with which it is at present their right to deal. I am sure they would not accept-and up to the present time they have shown no indication of any desire to accept-any fetters on their rights in this regard. That is why the agreements of the past between Canada and the United States, such as the one I have mentioned here, restrict the agreement to cooperation between the governments in all respects practicable to the extent of their respective executive powers. In my view there is no possibility that we could get the congress of the United States to agree to a set of principles in advance in order to deal with situations which could not be foreseen in advance, and which would restrict the activities and the rights of their legislative bodies.
I mentioned again, when dealing with this proposal previously, that there are already in existence many channels of communication between the United States and Canada, both formal and informal-and they were mentioned today by the Leader of the Opposition -by which the problems of the respective countries can be brought to the attention of the other in order that they may be dealt with in accordance with the legislative practices of the two countries. In regard to this particular problem it seems to me that the introduction of a further group in this connection would have a shackling effect on the relationship between the two countries. In view of the fact that we already have these many existing agencies for conveying international thoughts from Canada to the United States, the introduction of yet another would clog and confuse the present channels of communication. Each of the channels of communication would again have to refer to this document which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) wants to have formulated in order to make sure that their particular proposals fall in line with these principles.
It seems to me that the relations between this country and the United States, two great and expanding nations, cannot be fettered by this means in our future relationship. Surely it is wiser to ensure, as this government has done and as the Leader of the Opposition has acknowledged it has done since it came to

office, that the United States is made aware ol the determination of Canada to protect its sovereignty, its economic interests, and to assure in co-operation with the United States the survival of our two countries, as well as the countries of the NATO nations.
The Leader of the Opposition in making his submission dealt at very great length with this proposal of a new treaty between Canada and the United States. He based his remarks- indeed, the phraseology of the resolution supports this-upon the necessity of working out the implications of interdependence and closer unity within the North Atlantic community; at any rate, within a larger field than that of continental interdependence. He stressed that several times in the course of his remarks. I would suggest that the proposal that the Leader of the Opposition made in this regard would work exactly contrary to the expressed intentions of his motion. Surely the implications of such an agreement, if that were possible, would be such as to divide the European nations of NATO from us, and make them suspicious that there was developing such a division between the European and North Atlantic sides. In this regard I would like to refer to his speech of February 26, on page 1411, of Hansard, where he dealt with this particular problem. He said:
If we on this continent do not give some degree of consideration to and take some action about this development which is taking place in Europe-and I have said this a good many times-we will perhaps one of these days be faced with the division of the Atlantic world between the North American and European segments.
He goes on to say, quite rightly:
No one will gain from any division like that except those who are attempting to destroy the whole Atlantic community.
The very proposal that he has made today would be one which would tend to destroy the unity which there is in the NATO nations, and would divide them. In this regard I would like to refer to the record of what has gone on in this field of interdependence.
I would like to refer to what have been the developments in the years since the war in this portion of the world, which the Leader of the Opposition refers to as the North Atlantic community. In March, 1947, the economic and social council of the United Nations organization established the economic commission for Europe, whose aim was stated as being to initiate and participate in measures for facilitating concerted action for the economic reconstruction of Europe, for raising the level of European economic activity, and for maintaining and strengthening the economic relations of the European countries. Of course, its initial start was not a start which could have a life of great duration
Canadian-United States Relations because Soviet membership was included in that particular organization. Therefore it was necessary in 1948 to form the organization for European economic co-operation excluding the Soviet states.
Originally the O.E.E.C. aimed at enabling its members to co-operate closely in their economic relations and to formulate and execute a joint European recovery program based on Marshall Aid from the United States. As all hon. members will recall, the accomplishments of this body exceeded the hopes of its founders. Mutual consultation on economic policies among its members increased, and it carried out a program of trade liberalization. It stimulated production in its member countries and developed the European payments union to facilitate payment for articles of European commerce. Side by side with the attempts at economic revival, efforts were made to establish a new pattern of political and military co-operation.
The Dunkirk treaty of 1947, which bound Britain and France to resist any revival of German aggression, made way for the Brussels treaty of economic, social and cultural collaboration and collective self-defence, out of which developed western European union and provided for mutual defensive action by Britain, France and the Benelux countries in the event of an armed attack in Europe. I am going into this history, in order that we in Canada may recall at this time, in view of the comments made by the Leader of the Opposition, the record of the part which Canada took in those events in the past.

Mr. Speaker, before the six o'clock adjournment I had been dealing with the resolution which is proposed by the Leader of the Opposition and I referred to another proposal he made in his speech which was similar in character to that which he had proposed in this house on February 26 and to which I replied on the same date as reported at page 1435 of Hansard.
I also attempted in my earlier remarks to deal with the record that had been established in the field of interdependence arising out of the communist threat in the early postwar days. The purely national response to the threat of aggression in that period gave way after the treaty of Dunkirk of 1947 to the limited regional response of the western European union which in time was largely supplanted by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization with its much wider concept, an organization which in its original form had

Canadian-United, States Relations been thought of primarily as a military and political alliance embracing the fifteen member nations of NATO: Norway, Denmark, the Benelux countries, West Germany, Portugal, the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Germany and Iceland as well as Canada and the United States and extending as far east as Greece and Turkey.
Since the formation of NATO in April 1949 a number of other organizations have been created which to some extent perhaps have reduced the emphasis which might otherwise have been placed on development through NATO with respect to the ways and means to promote the non-military side of the alliance. There is, for example, the council of Europe which was launched in 1949-the talking shop of Europe as it has been called -an organization which has nevertheless been useful. Its purpose was to encourage social, economic and cultural co-operation among its members. It also had its intentions directed toward the formulation of European as opposed to purely national opinion.
There is the European coal and steel community of 1950, a remarkable and successful adventure in the creation of an organization which in itself has certain sovereign powers and rises in respect of those powers above the national states in whose territory it operates. More recently there has been the European economic community inaugurating a common market for its six member countries and finally the European atomic energy community, EURATOM, which aims to develop nuclear energy for peaceful uses with a view to raising the standards of living of its member states.
Much has been said in the past about the implementation of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty. I wish to make reference to a statement that appears at page 48 of the report of the Princeton University conference on NATO of June 1957:
Many specific proposals for expanding NATO's role in the economic sphere have been put forward by both official and private persons. But the facts are that NATO was not designed as an instrument for economic collaboration, and it has not acted as such an institution. The various suggestions that it do so have virtually come to naught.
In view of the existence of other organizations for economic co-operation the communique of the heads of government meeting in Paris in December of 1957 put its stand in these words:
We will accordingly lend encouragement to a successful development of the European economic committee and of a European free trade area.
I may say that apart from the purely military aspects of economic co-operation the emphasis has been to give importance to those

initiatives in such a way as to-and again I refer to the text of the communique:
-strengthen not only the participating countries, but also the relations within the Atlantic community and the free world as a whole.
In fact, clause 34 of that communique outlined what may be expected in the thinking of that time when it described the most that NATO can and should do in these words:
-without duplicating the work of other agencies, it should review from time to time economic trends and assess economic progress and make suggestions for improvement either through existing organizations, by the efforts of individual countries or in special cases by new initiatives.
I would recall to hon. members that last November the secretary general, Mr. Spaak, in addressing the NATO parliamentarians conference said:
A more competent body than NATO is necessary to face the Russian challenge for world domination in the political and economic fields.
He went on to say that at present the western nations:
-lack a body which would consider all economic angles, as the Russians are able to do. As a matter of fact-
He said,
-I do not even think that NATO should be this body for the needs in this sphere exceed the limits of our Atlantic alliance.
Mr. Spaak also said in a more general way:
NATO is no longer the perfect answer to the problem of communist expansion which it was when it came into being. The communist menace has now become more African and Asian than European, more economic than social and military.
Although we may not agree with Mr. Spaak's general interpretation of the situation, particularly in view of the present situation in Berlin where in fact military pressure is being threatened, nevertheless something of what he said points up a problem for Canada. Outside NATO the majority of the existing international organizations I have mentioned either attempt to deal with economic matters on a universal or worldwide scale or on the other hand are basically European rather than Atlantic and hence exclude Canada in the nature of their organization. The inverted protectionism of the common market excludes this country.
The O.E.E.C. excludes this country. All these organizations or proposals for organizations of European rather than Atlantic nature may assist in the recovery of Europe and for this we must be thankful. Those organizations were created or were in the process of being created at a time when the Leader of the Opposition was in the government of this country and when Canada's bargaining power in economic matters was never higher but still we were excluded.

Those were the days when the European nations were struggling to recover from the ravages of war and when for their very survival they depended upon Marshall aid, which was supplied by the United States. Never was there a time in the history of this country when Canada was in a better position to insist on interdependence than in those days. But now the Leader of the Opposition comes along and complains that this government should have been more active in working out the implications of interdependence and closer unity within the north Atlantic communities.
Those days I have mentioned, Mr. Speaker, were the days when he was in power, and it was at that time that those matters should have received his attention. Those days were different from the present, when the situation in the European countries has improved as a result of Marshall aid to the point where they have been restored in large part to the position they occupied before the war. Therefore, they are reasserting their independence in those matters. How much better would it have been if during those years when the Leader of the Opposition was a member of government, and at a time when Canada's bargaining position was never better in this field because of the economic weaknesses in the European countries which was brought about by the war, he had pushed the view then that he condemns the government for not pushing at this time?
The implications of western European economic integration are an aspect of this matter which I think deserve the consideration of this house. The two treaties of Rome, establishing respectively the European economic community and the European atomic energy community, were signed on March 25, 1957 by France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, Luxembourg and The Netherlands. They came into effect on January 1, 1958 and on January 1, of this year. The six signatories of the European economic community treaty put into effect among themselves a 10 per cent cut in tariffs and started to dismantle their remaining quantitative import restrictions.
These are the first steps which they took toward full customs union which it is proposed to establish in the course of a 12 to 15 year transitional period. At the end of that time, the six countries will thus form a free-trading area surrounded by a common external tariff and will also have undertaken a large degree of co-ordination of their commercial, social and financial policies, including the establishment of a European investment bank. Certain overseas territories of the member countries are associated with the community and will receive the benefits of the trade 66968-9-126

The other countries of western Europe have been apprehensive, as we in Canada have been apprehensive, lest the economic integration upon which the six have embarked create a grave economic and political division. Led by the United Kingdom, the remaining 11 members of the organization for European economic co-operation have accordingly striven for almost two years to negotiate some form of multilateral association with the six which would create a free-trading area among all 17 countries but which would leave each participant free to maintain its individual external tariff, and would stop short of the degree of integration aimed at by the European economic community. The efforts to reach agreement on the United Kingdom free-trade area proposals broke down in November, 1958. The commission of the European economic community is shortly, I understand, to produce a report suggesting how a multilateral association of the six and the 11 might be developed. In the meantime the United Kingdom and France are engaged in bilateral negotiations which may possibly provide a formula which could be used as a basis for a series of other bilateral arrangements intended to prevent the development of a discriminatory trading situation between those six on the one hand and the remaining members of the organization for European economic co-operation on the other.
The movement for European economic integration among the six at least has rested on the hope that by creating an economic unit comparable in size and resources with the United States they would be able to build up their economic efficiency and strength and by so doing would lay a foundation for an ultimate political integration. The free trade area countries, not being prepared to accept the long term political goal, have tended for their part to stress the disruptive effect which the emergence of an exclusive trading bloc in Europe might have on existing political cooperation. The same consideration would apply to co-operation within NATO, and for this reason it is of the utmost importance that any new economic relationships established in Europe, whether among six, or in the wider grouping of a free trade area, should be forward-looking and outward-looking and should not tend to create a regional and restrictive trading bloc.
In speaking in the budget debate on June 17, 1958, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has this to say:
The Canadian government is following with sympathy and interest these European efforts to

We attach high importance to the economic and political strength of western Europe as a safeguard of world peace and prosperity.
