This, Mr. Speaker, is the situation as I see it at the present time. The Leader of the Opposition, in his amendment, when viewed in the light of his speech, is contradictory, confused and completely woolly. On the one hand he advocates the taking of certain steps by Canada and the United States with regard to the relationship between our two countries which would tend to create on this side of the water an economic bloc, which would be divisive in so far as our NATO alliance is concerned. It completely fails to deal with the serious situation in which Canada finds herself as a result of the events of the years since the war for Canada, in her progress in those years, has found herself excluded from various organizations which have been formed in Europe. Admirable as they are in the purposes for which they were originally formed, namely to assist in the economic recovery of Europe, they do in fact not take account of Canada's vital interest in maintaining her trading relations with Europe.
After all these years, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition comes along with the amendment he has moved today, apparently in repentance for the past but with hope for the future. But in view of the woolly speech he made this afternoon in relation to the amendment before us I think it must be apparent to all members of the house that the ineffective suggestion he made can only have been made on the basis that the opposition can find so few thing about which to criticize the government that they have to fall back on this completely inadequate suggestion to bring before the house at this time. Repeatedly they have charged us with following courses that they thought were defective and have urged that the business of the house should be adjourned to discuss these various matters. But when they have an opportunity for a full debate, for full criticism of any of the government's policies, they bring forward this dismal production today and, as I said before, all members of the house can only be heartened by the effort they have made in that it is an assurance that there must be so little with respect to which they can criticize the present government.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment before the house is

in terms which I think justify repetition at this time after the beginning of the evening sitting. It is in these words:
This house is of the opinion that recent decisions of the United States government, particularly in the field of production and commercial policy, underline the necessity for the government to make more effective arrangements with the United States to prevent the undesirable impact of those decisions on Canada, and the necessity of a more active participation by the government in working out the implications of interdependence and closer unity within the North Atlantic community.
I regret that the hon. member who has just taken his seat should seemingly have misinterpreted the motive behind the action taken in the opening speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) which was intended to provide the house with the opportunity of discussing the important relations that prevail between our country and the United States, one of the most powerful, if not militarily and economically the most powerful country in the world today. The utterances of the Leader of the Opposition were, I think, couched in language which, while on occasion involving criticism of the administration in some particulars, was generally aimed, as the reactions of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) indicated, at the elucidation of a problem which increasingly is engaging the attention of serious-minded Canadians. As the Leader of the Opposition said, while all of our relations with friendly and not so friendly countries are important, it may be that in the complexity of modern life, both in terms of continental and other relationships, no bilateral relationship is as important as our relationship to the United States, both because of the fact that that country means a great deal to us in terms of our economic welfare and also because, through her position in world affairs, she is such a determinant factor in the easing of tension between nations and in the preservation of peace.
Therefore it is of the greatest importance that we should take advantage of opportunities such as this to assess the character of some of our problems as a result of our proximity to the United States, our association with her and our respective national ambitions and aspirations. Canadian-American relations have taken on an evolutionary form particularly in the last decade. For a long time we on both sides of the border referred with satisfaction to the fact that Canada and the United States in the Rush-Bagot treaty had developed possibly the first successful disarmament covenant among the nations. For a long time we have referred to the existence of the international joint commission as an

exemplar of our instrumentality in preserving peace between two nations and providing a method for adjudication of their differences and conflicts.
Then too, we have often mentioned the importance of the Ogdensburg discussions between the president of the United States and the prime minister of Canada during the days of the second world war and the Hyde Park agreement that had such significance in smoothing our common participation for the preservation of freedom and the resulting establishment as a result of the informal discussions between the president and our prime minister of the permanent board on defence, an organization which, having no more than the power of recommendation, nevertheless did lay down in the early stages of the postwar period the continental defence arrangements that have now taken on a more mature character.
Since that time, as a result of meetings between the presidents and the prime ministers, further instruments for joint collaboration and consideration have been created such as the ministerial committee dealing with economic affairs, the defence committee of interested ministers from the two governments and now finally, as a result of the last visit of the President of the United States and his conversations with the Prime Minister of today and his colleagues, the decision to set up, in collaboration with Your Honour and His Honour in the other place and opposite numbers in the congress of the United States, a congressional and parliamentary group which is intended to provide a further opportunity of informing both our legislative bodies about problems that are regarded as having mutual interest and concern. I think we must observe that these various instruments that have been created for these purposes can, if fully employed, render very satisfactory and useful service to the relations which we hope and believe and know will prevail notwithstanding all the difficulties between our two countries.
But I must say that I am sure hon. gentlemen sitting in the ministerial benches will concur that we do not altogether feel too happy about some of the meetings of the joint ministerial groups. The last meeting perhaps is the best example of some of the weaknesses in this particular arrangement. I note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has said it is hoped that on some occasion within the very near future this ministerial group will meet again, but quite obviously from the long communique that followed its deliberations a few months ago that medium, not without its value, did not come up to expectations which hon. gentlemen on all sides had for it.

It is with interest that I note from this report to which I have just made reference that until the middle of 1957 the main Canada-United States trade problem was the United States surplus disposal program on agricultural products which received its main impetus in 1954. I note that in commenting on some of the conclusions it is suggested by the Canadian-United States committee in a recent study that in the crop years 1954-55 over 40 per cent of the United States exports of agricultural commodities were aided under various governmental programs. With respect to wheat and wheat flour, virtually all such exports were subsidized and about one half moved under the stimulus of special disposal arrangements and the other half under the normal subsidies resulting from sales by the C.C.C. at prices below world levels. Now, the important matter that I wish to bring to the attention of the administration is that a new development has taken place in our commercial relations with the United States since the middle of 1957 when the

asked for an extension of time after February 28 in order to enable him to give further consideration as to whether or not the recommendation should receive the presidential veto.

I want to point out to the house, Mr. Speaker, that I believe that the developing problems in our country in connection with the United States are now such that the Prime Minister ought to give consideration to meeting with the President. It will be recalled that the President came to Canada last summer. He spoke in this house. We all recall that the reactions to his speech were not particularly acceptable to hon. gentlemen opposite. I am sure that both the President and the Prime Minister and the latter's colleagues profited greatly from their discussions with the President and with Mr. Dulles, the secretary of state for foreign affairs. But in view of the developing problems that are seemingly accruing now between our two countries on the economic front, and particularly in the matter of continental defence and defence purchases and their implications on our economic life, I wonder whether the Prime Minister will not give consideration to meeting the President at the earliest possible moment.
This is a matter in which Canadians generally are interested. It is not only the matter of the disposal of surplus commodities; it is not only the matter of embargo on our mineral deposits and the curbing of oil imports, there are gathering situations now which particularly arise as the result of the cancellation of the Arrow which placed us in a measure of increasing dependence on the productive capacity of the United States and on its defence arrangements.

I make that suggestion in the light particularly of the recommendations made by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon when he included among our concerns the situation with regard to uranium production in Canada. In view of the great stake that Canada has in uranium production and in view of the fact that our initiative and our resources went into this particular form of endeavour at a time when it meant so much in the prosecution of the war, we have, at least morally, a strong bargaining position which I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce will want to have placed before the authorities of the United States at the earliest possible moment so that we can await the reaction of that country to the events that will ensue in 1962 or 1963. In any event those are matters, together with the other matters which concern us, which warrant a meeting with the President of the United States.
I am sure that the house is not fully satisfied with the visit of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) in the matter of the application of extraterritorial powers by the government of the United States. All that the Minister of Justice was able to get from his opposite number in the United States was an assurance of consultation. There was no guarantee that such an infringement of our sovereignty would not occur again. I think that the Leader of the Opposition has proposed the only effective way to deal with that particular situation, and that is to embody in the form of solemn treaty the commitments in that and in other matters which the two governments are prepared to accept.
There is one other matter which I think, in a discussion of Canadian-United States relations, we cannot but carefully note at this time. I say this not without a full appreciation that when we were in power the United States was able to acquire certain rights in

D.E.W. line, the various preventative measures taken in that regard, the installation of radar and so on. All of those matters would be regarded in one sense as a violation of the principle of sovereignty. I think we have reached a stage in our relations with the United States when we have to think of the implications of our dependence upon that country for our security, and upon that country as the initiator of so much of what flows by way of economic buoyancy through defence contracts and the like.
When in 1948 the United States and Canada agreed to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and place themselves under the command of one responsible to a group of nations-the NATO commander-that was, on the part of the United States, a transfer of sovereignty. It was also a transfer of sovereignty on our part when we and they joined the United Nations. This country and all the members in that body, in the interests of the preservation of peace, transferred some of their sovereignty. That kind of transfer in our interdependent world is inevitable, and it is certainly desirable.
The Prime Minister of Great Britain will be here on Wednesday. When he was here last his theme was interdependence. He told us in this parliament that today all of the nations of the world were interdependent one of another. That did not mean that they were all equally involved in the mischief of war, but it did mean that in their common interest they had to pool their responsibilities, as well as the advantages which flowed from the international community. The Prime Minister of Great Britain will be here again, and this visit will give us the opportunity of once again emphasizing the significance and implication of his concept of interdependence.
So that when we joined NATO, and the United States and ourselves and other countries joined the United Nations, we recognized the force of interdependence in the world in which we live. But now we have to realize in Canada that the situation which confronted the European powers in 1948 in terms of contributions made by Canada and the United States now confronts Canada and the United States on the North American continent. Whatever power France or Great Britain has transferred to NATO has been transferred to a collective group of nations.
In the matter of our continental defence the transfer of sovereignty now from Canada to the United States is not to a collectivity; it is not to a grouping of nations; it is a transfer to one single power. We are now increasing our dependence on that power, and while we enjoy with that country the

I welcomed the efforts of the United Kingdom when they attempted to expand the European economic union to take in 17 Atlantic nations instead of only six. I only wish that the United Kingdom would have included the Dominion of Canada in a proposal of this type.
Our problem is, where do we stand now? The European economic union ruled us out. We have a serious problem on our hands. The United States economy is largely selfsufficient; the western European nations are beginning to look after themselves and do not have to depend on us. We feel that we should take more aggressive measures for the sponsoring of a real, effective north Atlantic economic community either with or without the United States of America.
I remember very well a really worthwhile speech made in this House of Commons on this subject some years ago by the former member for Winnipeg North, Alistair Stewart. His proposal at
tMr. Regier.]

that time to the House of Commons was that the member nations of NATO should reach an agreement whereby they would progressively reduce their tariff barriers, one NATO nation to another, by a flat percentage of 10 per cent per annum. His argument was that that would not be so severe that member nations would not be able to afford to smooth over the hardships that might be imposed by dislocations in each of the participating nations. Then his argument was that we could look forward to the day when the whole western world as we now know it would be one economic unit with a fairly uniform standard of living for all of its people. This would lead to closer social, cultural and he hoped eventually political, ties.
I do not see this as running counter to the interests of world brotherhood, because if we are to build world brotherhood, we have to begin to build it with our immediate neighbours and with people who are most closely allied with us. When we have established some feeling of brotherhood there-a brotherhood, I may say, based on more than military alliances-then we can begin to proceed with more assurance toward establishing a world brotherhood.
Our present method of going about things in the western world, Mr. Speaker, is going to give us cause for regret in the not too distant future. The United States government, if it wants to be loyal to the interests of its own people in the western world as it exists today, cannot give us treatment which is very radically different from what we are receiving today. I also feel that if we are going to allow the European economic union to operate for any number of years, it is going to become more and more difficult for us to ally ourselves with the economy of western Europe. I feel that the longer we postpone closer economic ties with member nations of the commonwealth, the more difficult it is going to be for us to cement those ties, because they are not exploring ways and means of allying their economic lives with the economic lives of other parts of the world.
I feel that we have done ourselves a lot more harm than good over the past five years by protesting so loudly yet never being prepared to follow up any protest with any action. We have established much ill will south of the border. We have deliberately- I blame in the main the former Liberal government for this-alienated ourselves from the markets of Europe, the United Kingdom and the commonwealth. I regret that I fail to see any substantial action which

has come out of this government in the past eighteen months of its life to indicate that there has been any fundamental and basic change. They, like the former government, keep on running to Washington hoping that they will get a better deal out of Washington. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that that better deal is going to be a long, long time in showing itself.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Office of the Commissioner Ottawa
March 12, 1959.
The Hon. E. D. Fulton, Q.C., M.P.,
Minister of Justice,
OTTAWA, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Fulton:
On Sunday last you received a wire from the attorney general of Newfoundland asking under the terms of the contract that 50 R.C.M. Police reinforcements be sent to that province for duty in areas where the loggers are on strike. At about the same time I received a telephone call from Superintendent A. W. Parsons, the officer commanding the R.C.M. Police in Newfoundland, advising me of the situation and informing me that he had requested the attorney general to apply for help.
Superintendent Parsons told me that he might be able to get some assistance from the Newfoundland constabulary, the provincial force which polices St. John's, and I asked that he follow up on this possibility at once in the hope that help from that quarter might avoid the necessity of sending in reinforcements from outside.
I discussed the situation with you during the afternoon by telephone. I also received a further call from Superintendent Parsons letting me know that he had been able to get a detail of 25 men from the Newfoundland constabulary and had also scraped up another 20 from his own resources. With this help he felt that his request for reinforcements from outside might be held in abeyance.
On Tuesday, March 10, at your request I dispatched the following message to Superintendent Parsons:
Please deliver following message to Mr. Curtis begins re your tel. March 8 to Minister of Justice Stop Mr. Fulton has referred matter to me with instructions to watch situation closely Stop Have accordingly taken steps necessary to insure that RCMP reinforcements are ready with air transport available Stop I am advised changing situation including steps taken within provincial establishment and help from constabulary indicate reinforcements from outside province may not now be needed Stop Accordingly situation will be watched closely and readiness maintained pending further developments ends
At 11 o'clock Tuesday evening, March 10, Superintendent Parsons informed me of the clash which had just taken place on the highway outside the town of Badger between approximately 300 strikers armed with clubs, bottles and other weapons, and a detail of about 50 police including 15 men of the Newfoundland constabulary. Parsons felt that this clash might be the turning point and might convince the strikers that the police were determined to maintain law and order.
At about 6 a.m. yesterday Parsons telephoned me again and told me that instead of improving the situation in the Badger area was deteriorating. Another 100 men had come in during the night and the total number of strikers in this little town now stood at about 400. These were almost all from outside points.
At 8:30 a.m. yesterday I informed you of the situation and, with your approval, took steps to get a body of 50 men ready in the maritimes and to arrange for air transportation. Later you asked that the plane be held at Moncton where some of the men were to be gathered until the cabinet had time to consider the Newfoundland request. At about 5:20 p.m. you informed me that the cabinet had decided the request from Newfoundland was to be refused. I thereupon told you that I could not understand or agree with the decision and that I would let you have my resignation the following morning.
The clause in the contract dealing with the provision of reinforcements is to my mind quite clear. It reads as follows:
Where in the opinion of the attorney general of the province an emergency exists within the province requiring additional members of the force to assist in dealing with such emergency, Canada shall, at the request of the attorney general of the province addressed to the commissioner, increase the strength of the division as requested if in the opinion of the Attorney General of Canada, having regard to other responsibilities and duties of the force, such increase is possible.
There is no doubt in my mind as to the need and I am certain that the number of men asked for can be provided without prejudice to "other responsibilities and duties."
I realize that other issues are before you which arise from this strike but I feel most strongly that the matter of law enforcement should be isolated and dealt with on

its own merits. This is the attitude the force has taken throughout. It has not concerned itself with the issues back of the strike but has merely tried to maintain law and order in the area.
I think the contract clause on this matter of providing reinforcements in an emergency is clear and I cannot escape the conclusion that failure to supply reinforcements in this instance is a breach of that clause. Bearing in mind that we have similar contracts with seven other provinces the decision of the government has a particular significance.
With these considerations in mind I feel I have no option but to ask you to accept my resignation and this I now do. I hope you will be able to relieve me as soon as possible and I shall await your advice as to what arrangements will be made to that end.
I cannot close without telling you how much I regret having to take this step. I am within a year of completing my full service and I had looked forward to finishing my time in a more pleasant way. I have enjoyed serving under your direction and I have appreciated your support of the force and your active interest and understanding in all aspects of its work. I assure you that it is only a firm conviction of the correctness of my view which leads me to take this disagreeable action.
Yours sincerely,
L. H. Nicholson
(L. H. Nicholson), Commissioner.

Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
Ottawa, Canada,
March 16th, 1959.
Commissioner L. H. Nicholson,
Royal Canadian Mounted Police,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Commissioner Nicholson,
I have received your letter of March 12 and have learned with regret your decision to submit your resignation as commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
You first indicated your intention to resign on Wednesday evening, March 11. This was in the course of a telephone conversation, immediately after I had informed you of the decision that the reinforcements requested by the attorney general of Newfoundland should not be sent at that time. My recollection of the developments leading up to that point is in accordance with the
facts as set out in your letter of March 12, with one minor exception to which I shall refer later.
The fundamental difference between us, as I view the matter, centers around your conclusion that there has been a breach of the clause quoted by you from the contract between Canada and Newfoundland.
The obligation imposed on Canada by that clause is to increase the number of members of the force in the province if, in my opinion as Attorney General of Canada, "having regard to other responsibilities and duties of the force," such increase is possible.
In reaching my conclusion on the question whether "having regard to other responsibilities and duties of the force", such increase were possible, I, of course, as you know, gave the most careful and anxious consideration to your views that additional members could and should be sent to Newfoundland without prejudice to other responsibilities and duties of the force. However, upon a consideration of all the factors, including especially the importance of preserving the character and capacity of the force to discharge its duty in connection with law enforcement in all of Canada, I came to the conclusion, after consulting my colleagues, that, as the situation existed at that time, it was not possible to send the additional men requested without prejudicing the other responsibilities and duties of the force.
This decision was my responsibility. I reached it only after the most careful consideration of your views and of all the other factors that, in my judgment, were relevant. I regret profoundly that you came to the conclusion that, by reason of that decision, you should resign.
Much as I regret your decision to tender your resignation, under these circumstances I have no alternative but to accept it and am prepared to make a submission to the governor in council accordingly. However, there will be a number of administrative arrangements that must be made to meet the situation thereby created, and I shall appreciate it if you will carry on until such time as a successor can be appointed. I expect this will be in the very near future.
While the point of minor difference to which I referred at the beginning of this letter may not be of any real significance, I should mention it for the purposes of the record. It is my clear recollection of our conversation at 5:20 p.m. on March 11 last, that I informed you that the decision taken as of that time was that the dispatch of reinforcements was to be delayed pending further consideration, and not that it had

been finally decided to refuse the request, as appears from the third paragraph on page 2 of your letter. I appreciate that, from your point of view, this difference may not be of any significance in its implication. Nevertheless I thought that I ought to mention it.
It remains only for me to express my deep personal regret that you should feel impelled to make this decision. You know that I disagree with your view as to the course you should follow but I respect the sincerity and conviction with which you
hold it. I have enjoyed our association since I became minister responsible for the force and have appreciated your advice and support and the very pleasant relationship we have enjoyed in every aspect of the work of the force. You can rest assured that whatever may be the views as to the present situation you have earned the respect and esteem of all those with whom you have served.
Yours sincerely,
E.	D. Fulton.
Tuesday, March 17, 1959
